title: Report revenue per visitor and contribution per visitor next to conversion rate
hypothesis: If we report RPV and contribution per visitor next to conversion rate on every test, then the team stops shipping changes that raise conversion but cut order value or margin, because RPV multiplies rate by AOV and contribution multiplies RPV by margin.

signal.check: Dashboards and test readouts show conversion rate alone, with no AOV or margin line next to it.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source claims it stops false wins rather than states a lift

risk.note: This is a reporting change, not a site change, so there is little to reverse.

prerequisites: GA4 session and order data
gross margin by SKU or category
steps: Pull GA4 sessions, Shopify orders and net revenue for the period.
Compute RPV as conversion rate times AOV.
Compute contribution per visitor as RPV times gross margin percent.
Add both numbers to every dashboard and test readout template.

test.method: Not a test on its own; apply it as the reporting standard for every future test.
test.measure: RPV and contribution per visitor next to conversion rate

title: Stop comparing conversion rate across brands or using it as the goal
hypothesis: If we treat conversion rate as a diagnostic only and never compare it to another brand's number, then the team stops chasing a rate that a price cut or traffic shift can move on its own, because rate depends on category, price, traffic mix and product quality.

signal.check: A report or a founder benchmarks the store's conversion rate against a competitor or an industry number.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the point is to stop misreading it, not to move it

risk.note: Reporting habit only.

steps: Remove any slide or dashboard that ranks this store's conversion rate against another brand.
Replace external benchmarks with the store's own trend over time.
When rate moves, check traffic mix, price and category before concluding the page changed anything.

test.method: No test; a reporting rule.
test.measure: Whether readouts still cite outside benchmarks

title: Rebuild revenue, AOV and conversion numbers with the correct inputs
hypothesis: If we use net sales plus shipping collected, GA4 sessions and orders divided by GA4 sessions, then every RPV and conversion figure gets more accurate, because Shopify's raw totals include tax and bot-heavy sessions.

signal.check: Reports use Shopify 'Total sales' or Shopify sessions instead of GA4 sessions and net revenue.

expected_effect.size: corrected conversion rate should read higher than the Shopify-session version

risk.note: A recalculation, not a site change.

prerequisites: Shopify analytics access
GA4 access
steps: Pull Net sales plus Shipping collected, or Total sales minus tax, for revenue.
Divide that revenue by orders for a corrected AOV.
Pull GA4 sessions for the same period instead of Shopify sessions.
Compute conversion rate as corrected orders divided by GA4 sessions.
Note the gap between GA4 and Shopify sessions so it is not re-litigated later.

test.method: Not a test; a one-time and then recurring recalculation.
test.measure: Corrected RPV and conversion rate versus the old Shopify-only numbers
test.read_point: Before the next funnel read or test brief

title: Track RPV as a long trend, never as a single point, and keep CAC out of it
hypothesis: If we chart RPV over months instead of reading one week, and keep ad spend out of the calculation, then the team can see a real shift instead of reacting to noise, because a single-period read hides normal week to week swings.

signal.check: RPV or contribution per visitor is quoted from a single week with no trend line.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source names about 2.5 years as its own trend window

risk.note: Reporting habit only.

prerequisites: Historical GA4 and order data
steps: Build a monthly RPV and contribution-per-visitor trend line.
Keep CAC and ad spend out of the contribution-per-visitor number itself.
Read LTGP to CAC and contribution profit alongside the trend, not inside it.

test.method: No test; a dashboard build.
test.measure: Monthly RPV trend versus point-in-time RPV

title: Pick conversion rate, RPV or gross profit per visitor as primary by the store's traffic band
hypothesis: If we use conversion rate as primary below about 3,000 orders a month and RPV or gross profit above it, then test results get read with the right amount of statistical power, because RPV needs about 6 times the traffic conversion rate needs to detect the same relative effect.

signal.check: A test brief names RPV or gross profit as the primary metric while the store runs under 300 to 3,000 orders a month.

expected_effect.size: RPV needs about 6x the traffic of conversion rate for the same relative MDE (about 175,000 vs 28,000 visitors per variant at 3% baseline)

risk.note: A sizing rule, not a site change.

prerequisites: Monthly order count
baseline conversion rate
steps: Count orders per month for the page or audience in question.
Under 300 orders a month: conversion rate primary, RPV and AOV as guardrails.
300 to 3,000: conversion rate primary is still safer; RPV is borderline.
3,000 or more: RPV as primary is workable, winsorized.
Write the choice and the reason into the test brief.

test.method: Not a test; a sizing decision written into every brief.
test.measure: Whether the brief's primary metric matches the order band

title: Set guardrail thresholds and require them to hold before calling any test a win
hypothesis: If we require AOV, gross margin, return rate, refund rate, page load and downstream purchase to hold flat or improve, then a conversion win that quietly hurts profit or LTV never ships as a win, because a single metric can be gamed while others move against the store.

signal.check: A test readout reports the primary metric moved with no mention of AOV, margin or return rate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; guardrails prevent false wins rather than create a lift

risk.note: A brief and readout requirement.

prerequisites: Baseline AOV, margin, return and refund rate
steps: List the standard guardrails: AOV, gross margin, return rate, refund rate, page load, add to cart, downstream purchase.
Add returns, chargebacks, repeat rate and 365-day LTV by angle before scaling any winning angle.
Set a threshold for each guardrail before the test launches.
In the readout, report every guardrail, not only the primary metric.

test.method: Not a test; a brief and readout requirement applied to every test.
test.read_point: At test close, before shipping a win

title: Use a micro-conversion as primary only for low-volume or far-from-purchase tests, with a purchase guardrail
hypothesis: If a low-volume store or a change far from purchase uses add-to-cart or CTA-click rate as primary with purchase as a guardrail, then the team gets a faster read without banking a lift that never reaches revenue, because a step near purchase is the one that actually pays.

signal.check: The store runs 30 to 300 orders a month, or the tested step is far from purchase (a homepage module, a collection filter).

risk.note: A micro-conversion lift with no purchase check can be banked as a false win.

prerequisites: Weekly traffic and orders on the tested page
steps: Check monthly orders and how close the tested step sits to purchase.
If under 300 orders a month, or the step is far from purchase, choose a micro-conversion as primary.
Set purchase and revenue as guardrails in the same brief.
Never bank the micro-conversion lift without checking the purchase guardrail at close.

test.method: A/B test with a micro-conversion as primary metric and purchase as guardrail.
test.measure: Add-to-cart rate, checked against purchase rate
test.read_point: At planned sample or 2 to 4 weeks

title: Rank the backlog and read tests by gross profit per conversion, not raw revenue
hypothesis: If we weight ranking and readouts by gross profit per conversion instead of revenue, then a change that shifts sales toward low-margin SKUs stops looking like a win, because revenue can rise while profit falls.

signal.check: A backlog or an offer test is ranked or read by revenue lift alone with no margin check.

risk.note: A scoring change.

prerequisites: Gross margin by SKU or category
steps: Get gross margin by SKU or category from finance.
Recompute backlog expected value using gross profit per conversion, not revenue.
Re-read any offer or mix test on contribution, not AOV alone.

test.method: No test; a scoring and reading rule for every offer or mix test.
test.read_point: At ranking time and at test close

title: Judge a CRO programme or agency by holdout-measured incremental value, not test volume
hypothesis: If a CRO retainer or in-house programme is judged by incremental revenue against a holdout, then the founder stops paying for activity that would have happened anyway, because a count of shipped tests says nothing about causal value.

signal.check: A programme review reports number of tests shipped with no holdout-based incremental number.

risk.note: A reporting standard for the programme, not a site change.

prerequisites: A programme holdout in place (see programme holdout idea)
steps: Ask 'would this have happened anyway' before crediting any monthly result to CRO.
Require a programme holdout readout before renewing or judging a retainer.
Stop using test count alone as a success metric.

test.method: Programme holdout comparison, see CRO-089.
test.measure: Net incremental revenue or margin from the holdout
test.read_point: At programme review, at least quarterly

title: Pitch CRO work to the founder through CAC and the revenue equation, not conversion rate alone
hypothesis: If we frame a CRO investment as a CAC reduction (CAC is about ad spend divided by sessions times conversion rate), then the founder can compare it against more ad spend on the same basis, because a conversion lift lets spend rise back to the old CAC ceiling.

signal.check: A CRO proposal or budget request cites conversion rate alone with no CAC or revenue-equation framing.

expected_effect.size: a conversion lift cuts CAC in proportion

risk.note: A framing change for an internal pitch.

prerequisites: Current CAC and conversion rate
steps: State CAC as ad spend divided by sessions times conversion rate.
Show how a conversion lift lowers CAC and lets spend rise back to the old ceiling.
Reference revenue = traffic x conversion rate x AOV x repeat rate, and name which 3 of 4 CRO controls.
Note that doubling conversion is rare; set expectations against realistic lifts (R77).

test.method: No test; an internal business case.
test.measure: CAC before and after a shipped win

title: Read the full funnel and find the single biggest weighted leak before choosing any fix
hypothesis: If we instrument sessions through purchase by device and channel and weight each drop by traffic and value, then the team works on the stage that actually costs the most revenue, because a 10-point drop on the hero PDP outranks a 30-point drop on a page with little traffic.

signal.check: No current funnel memo names the biggest weighted leak by device and channel.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a diagnosis step, not a lift on its own

risk.note: A read, not a change.

prerequisites: GA4 Explore funnel configured
tracking confirmed accurate
steps: In GA4 Explore, build a funnel: product view, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase.
For paid traffic, extend the map: ad, landing page, PDP, cart, checkout, thank-you, post-purchase upsell.
Read each stage rate by device and channel.
Weight each drop by the sessions and revenue passing through it.
Write the funnel memo naming the biggest weighted leak.

test.method: Not a test; a diagnostic read done before any change.
test.measure: Stage conversion rates by device and channel, weighted by traffic
test.read_point: Before the first test, and after every shipped change

title: Compare funnel stage rates against the reference bands, but treat them as directional only
hypothesis: If we compare each stage rate against the poor to excellent bands and then check traffic intent and device mix before blaming design, then a low band gets the right diagnosis, because the bands come from one unsourced source, not a study.

signal.check: A stage looks poor or average against the bands (overall under 1 to 3%, add to cart under 5 to 12%, cart to checkout under 30 to 60%, checkout completion under 50 to 70%).

risk.note: A read, not a change.

prerequisites: Funnel memo from CRO-011
steps: Compare each stage rate to the bands: overall, add to cart, cart to checkout, checkout completion.
Before concluding a stage is broken, check traffic intent, cold-traffic share and device mix.
Treat a below-band stage as a hypothesis to investigate, not a proven defect.

test.method: Not a test; a benchmarking check.
test.measure: Stage rate versus band, after mix is ruled out

title: Watch recordings, heatmaps or a survey on the exact leaking step before writing a hypothesis
hypothesis: If we always watch the specific step that shows a funnel drop before writing a fix, then the hypothesis addresses why shoppers leave, not just where, because a funnel drop only shows the location, not the cause.

signal.check: A hypothesis is written straight from a funnel drop with no recording, heatmap or survey behind it.

risk.note: A research step, not a change.

prerequisites: Behaviour tool access
survey in place or bootstrapped
steps: Name the exact step where the funnel drop occurs.
Watch recordings or read a heatmap for that step.
Cross-check against survey answers for the same step.
Write the hypothesis only after at least one of these confirms a cause.

test.method: Not a test; a research gate before writing a hypothesis.
test.measure: Whether the hypothesis names its evidence

title: Diagnose traffic mix before redesigning a page after a conversion-rate move
hypothesis: If we split conversion by traffic temperature before touching a page, then a redesign only happens when a segment's own rate actually fell, because a rising cold-traffic share can lower the blended rate with no page change at all.

signal.check: A redesign is requested because blended conversion rate fell, with no segment breakdown yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids wasted redesign work rather than lifting a number directly

risk.note: A read, not a change.

prerequisites: Conversion rate segmented by cold paid, warm and returning traffic
steps: Split conversion rate by cold paid, warm and returning traffic.
Check whether cold traffic's share of sessions rose in the period.
Check returning-customer share, since it inflates blended conversion and AOV.
Check category, price point, AOV, creative and offer changes in the same window.
Only audit the page if one segment's own rate fell with steady creative; otherwise report a mix effect and stop.

test.method: Not a test; a diagnostic split done before any redesign brief.
test.measure: Segment-level conversion rate versus blended rate
test.read_point: Any time blended conversion rate triggers a redesign request

title: Fix checkout completion as repairs first, before touching earlier funnel steps
hypothesis: If checkout completion is the biggest weighted leak, we fix it first, mostly as repairs, because Baymard figures suggest a large share of checkout uplift comes from UX fixes on a typical site.

signal.check: Checkout completion sits in the poor or average band from the funnel read.

expected_effect.size: about 35% checkout uplift available from UX fixes alone, per Baymard as cited (verify current figures)

risk.note: Repairs are lower risk than tests; most cannot be A/B tested on standard Shopify anyway.

prerequisites: Funnel read naming checkout as the leak
Shopify plan tier known
steps: Confirm checkout completion is poor or average against the bands.
List known checkout friction: extra costs, forced accounts, missing express pay, long fields.
Ship fixes as repairs, since most checkout changes cannot be A/B tested on standard Shopify plans.
Measure with before-and-after stage rates as weak evidence, not a controlled test.

test.method: Before-and-after stage-rate comparison (weak evidence, not a randomised test).
test.read_point: A few weeks after the repair ships

title: Confirm tracking health before trusting any funnel read or test launch
hypothesis: If we compare event counts against backend orders before every funnel read and test launch, then a broken or double-firing event never invalidates a decision silently, because missing or inconsistent events make any downstream read wrong.

signal.check: Funnel event counts have not been compared against store backend orders recently.

risk.note: A check, not a change.

prerequisites: GA4 and Shopify backend access
steps: Compare GA4 event counts with orders in the store backend for the same period.
If counts do not match within a few percent, stop and route to fixing tracking before any funnel read.
Recheck before every test launch, since broken tracking mid-test invalidates the result.

test.method: Not a test; a tracking QA check.
test.measure: Event count versus backend order count
test.read_point: Before every funnel read and test launch

title: Check collection page exit rate against the site average before assuming a design problem
hypothesis: If we check traffic intent before redesigning a collection page with a high exit rate, then design work only happens where intent is already good, because a high exit rate can mean the visitor wanted something else, not that the page is broken.

signal.check: A collection page shows a materially higher exit rate than the site average.

risk.note: A read, not a change.

prerequisites: Collection pages with material traffic
steps: Pull exit rate for each collection page with material traffic.
Compare against the site average.
Check traffic source and intent before assuming a design problem.
Only then move to the collection page checklist for design fixes.

test.method: Not a test; a diagnostic read.
test.measure: Collection exit rate versus site average

title: Audit every PDP and collection page with material direct entrances as its own landing page
hypothesis: If we treat pages with a material share of direct entrances as cold-traffic landing pages, then those pages carry their own proof and delivery information instead of relying on homepage context, because search and ads often send people straight to an inner page that never shows homepage trust signals.

signal.check: The landing-page report has not been checked for which PDPs or collections get a material share of direct entrances.

does_not_apply_when: Store has almost no direct entrances to inner pages

risk.note: Adding proof and delivery info to a page has little downside.

prerequisites: Landing-page report showing entrance page by traffic
steps: Pull the landing-page report to find which PDPs and collections get direct entrances.
For each such page, check whether proof, delivery info and trust signals are present without scrolling to the homepage.
Add proof and delivery info directly on pages that lack it.
Re-check after the change.

test.method: Ship as a repair or, if traffic allows, an A/B test on the affected pages.

title: Verify sessions, conversion rate and revenue definitions match across every report before comparing them
hypothesis: If every report uses the same session source and revenue definition, then two reports never disagree for a reason that has nothing to do with the store, because Shopify and GA4 count sessions and revenue differently.

signal.check: Two reports for the same period show different conversion rates or revenue with no explanation.

risk.note: A reconciliation check.

prerequisites: GA4 and Shopify analytics access
steps: List every recurring report that cites sessions, conversion rate or revenue.
Confirm each one uses GA4 sessions and net revenue plus shipping, not Shopify raw totals.
Fix any report using a different definition.

test.method: Not a test; a reconciliation pass.
test.read_point: Once, then whenever a new report is built

title: Require at least 2 points of evidence before any hypothesis enters the backlog
hypothesis: If every hypothesis needs analytics plus one of a replay, heatmap, survey or user test before it enters the backlog, then the backlog fills with ideas that are more likely to win, because a store with pre-qualified hypotheses reports a much higher win rate than one running on opinion.

signal.check: The backlog has ideas with only one source, or only an opinion, behind them.

expected_effect.size: one source cites a 36.3% win rate tied to pre-qualifying with analytics, recordings and heatmaps

risk.note: A backlog rule, not a site change.

prerequisites: Analytics access
at least one behaviour or research tool
steps: For every backlog entry, list which evidence points support it.
Require analytics plus at least one of a replay, heatmap, survey or user test.
Reject or hold any entry that only has an opinion behind it.

test.method: Not a test; a backlog admission rule.
test.measure: Win rate of gated versus ungated ideas over time

title: Run the non-negotiable research stack before the store's first test
hypothesis: If every store runs a funnel drop-off analysis, a PDP heatmap, a rage-click check, a post-purchase survey and review mining before its first test, then the first hypotheses are backed by more than a guess, because these five inputs are named as non-negotiable at any traffic level.

signal.check: The store has never run a funnel analysis, a PDP heatmap, a post-purchase survey or review mining.

risk.note: Research work, not a site change.

prerequisites: Behaviour tool installed
review app if 500+ reviews
steps: Run a funnel drop-off analysis (see funnel read idea).
Set up a heatmap on the PDP.
Check for false-click and rage-click patterns.
Set up or check the post-purchase survey.
Mine reviews once the store has 500 to 1,000 or more reviews.
Allow about 1 to 2 weeks to gather this under 300,000 monthly sessions.

test.method: Not a test; a one-time and then recurring research setup.
test.measure: Whether all 5 inputs exist and are current
test.read_point: Before the first test, and refreshed periodically

title: Use behaviour data to prioritise a hypothesis, never to claim a proven lift
hypothesis: If heatmaps, scroll maps and recordings are only used to prioritise which hypothesis to write, then no one claims a conversion or revenue lift from behaviour data alone, because these tools show behaviour, not statistical proof.

signal.check: A finding from a heatmap or recording is presented as a proven impact with no sample-size math behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this prevents a false claim rather than creating a lift

risk.note: A discipline rule.

steps: Use behaviour data to prioritise which page or hypothesis to work on.
Apply sample-size math (see the test-sizing idea) before claiming any impact.
Never state a conversion or revenue number from a heatmap or recording alone.

test.method: Not a test; a claims discipline rule.
test.measure: Whether readouts cite sample math behind any claimed impact

title: Start every heatmap or recording review by naming the page's one core action
hypothesis: If every page review starts by naming the one core action and asking whether people reach it, take it, and what would get them there, then the review stays focused on what actually moves revenue, because an unstructured review can drift into noticing anything.

signal.check: A heatmap or recording review has no named core action for the page.

risk.note: A method step, not a change.

prerequisites: Behaviour tool access
steps: Name the page's one core action: add to cart, buy now, start checkout, or sign up.
Ask whether people reach that section.
Ask whether they take the action.
If not, ask what would get them there.

test.method: Not a test; a research method step.
test.measure: Whether the review names a core action and its 3 questions

title: Read rage clicks, dead clicks and scroll behaviour from Insights, and top-line metrics from GA4
hypothesis: If we take rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling and quick backs from Clarity's Insights, and sessions, scroll depth and channel splits from GA4, then each tool is used for what it does best, because Clarity's own top-line metrics duplicate GA4 with less accuracy.

signal.check: A report cites Clarity's own session or channel numbers instead of GA4's.

risk.note: A tool-usage rule.

prerequisites: Clarity or Hotjar installed
GA4 access
steps: Open the Insights block in Clarity for rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling and quick backs.
Pull sessions, scroll depth, pages per session, channel and device from GA4.
Use Clarity's own top-line numbers only as context, not as the report of record.

test.method: Not a test; a tool-usage rule.
test.measure: Consistency of source per metric type

title: Watch the recordings behind a rate before acting on it, and never ignore a real defect for a low rate
hypothesis: If a percentage from Clarity Insights is checked against its recordings before acting, then the team fixes real usability issues even at a low rate and avoids chasing a rate with no clear cause, because a percentage alone does not say whether the issue matters.

signal.check: A rage-click, dead-click or scroll rate is acted on, or dismissed, with no recordings watched.

risk.note: A research discipline step.

prerequisites: Clarity or Hotjar access
steps: For every Insight rate, click through to the matching recordings.
If a real usability issue shows, fix it regardless of the rate.
If the rate is low with no clear issue in the recordings, do not prioritise it.

test.method: Not a test; a research discipline step.
test.measure: Whether every acted-on rate has recordings cited

title: Classify rage clicks, dead clicks, scrolling and quick backs by what the shopper expected before fixing them
hypothesis: If we classify each behaviour signal by what the shopper likely expected (blocked exit, useful missing action, buried information, false click), then the fix addresses the real cause, because the same signal type can come from very different problems.

signal.check: A behaviour signal is flagged with no classification of its likely cause.

expected_effect.size: one source reports massive wins from removing false-click elements in high-volume stores; no figure given

risk.note: A classification step, then a repair.

prerequisites: Recordings for the same page and device
steps: For rage clicks, check for a popup, chat widget or hard-to-close control in the way.
For dead clicks, check if the missing action would help the purchase (broken logo, gallery image, single working button).
For excessive scrolling or quick backs, check for missing or buried information.
For elements styled like buttons that do nothing, flag as a false click to fix or restyle.
Confirm the cause in recordings for the same page and device before treating it as a pattern.

test.method: Repair once confirmed as a defect (see R50); otherwise a hypothesis for a test.
test.measure: Rage or dead click rate after the fix
test.read_point: After the fix ships, in fresh recordings

title: Read scroll reach and click share together to find placement and relevance problems
hypothesis: If we read a module's click share against how far down the page it sits, then a high-click low-reach module gets tested higher up, because placement, not the module itself, may be hiding real demand.

signal.check: A module has a high share of clicks but is reached by a much smaller share of visitors, or a highly visible module gets few clicks.

expected_effect.size: one case reports an 18% conversion lift after moving a module up, with no statistics given

risk.note: A layout move, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Area map and scroll map for the page
steps: Read scroll reach at the top, average fold, 75%, 50% and 25%.
Read click share per module from the Area map.
Flag modules with high click share and low reach.
Flag highly visible modules with few clicks.
Confirm intent versus confusion in recordings for the flagged elements.
Write the hypothesis to move the module, keeping the design and destination the same.

test.method: A/B test: same module design and destination, only the position changes.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart or purchase conversion, with behaviour as support

title: Weight heatmap clicks by revenue or click share, never by raw counts
hypothesis: If we weight heatmap clicks by revenue where the tool allows, and by click share otherwise, then priority goes to modules that matter to revenue, because raw click counts favour high-traffic pages regardless of value.

signal.check: A heatmap finding is reported as a raw click count with no revenue or share weighting.

risk.note: A reading rule.

prerequisites: Heatmap tool with area or revenue-tied reporting
steps: Check whether the heatmap tool can weight clicks by revenue per click.
If yes, use it for prioritisation.
If not, use Clarity's Area map click share by region instead of raw counts.

test.method: Not a test; a reading rule.
test.measure: Whether findings cite share or revenue weighting

title: Run structured recording review sessions with no quota, and stop when patterns repeat
hypothesis: If recording reviews block 1 to 2 focused hours, compare engaged with disengaged sessions, and stop once patterns repeat, then the review finds real patterns without wasting time on redundant sessions, because a fixed quota can stop too early or run too long.

signal.check: Recordings are watched with no plan for volume, sorting or stopping point.

risk.note: A research method.

prerequisites: Recording tool with filters and sort
steps: Filter recordings by time frame, device, action, scroll depth and landing page.
Sort by clicks and pages high to low, then reverse, and compare the two groups on the same page type.
Block 1 to 2 hours with no distractions and note every key finding.
Ask 'why' about every action seen.
Stop when new sessions repeat patterns already logged.
After a fix ships, repeat with fresh recordings of the new version.

test.method: Not a test; a research method for building hypotheses.
test.measure: Number of confirmed patterns per session block
test.read_point: Every research round, and after every ship

title: Fix the heatmap screenshot and filter by the top device before reading a heatmap
hypothesis: If we confirm the heatmap screenshot shows the real page and filter by the device with the most traffic, then the reading reflects what shoppers actually see, because a captured popup or a minority device can distort every finding.

signal.check: A heatmap has not been checked for a captured popup or broken layout before reading.

risk.note: A QA step.

prerequisites: Heatmap tool access
device split known
steps: Open the heatmap and check the screenshot for a popup or broken layout.
If wrong, use Change screenshot to pick another version.
Filter by the device with the most traffic first.
Read the scroll map at top, average fold, 75%, 50% and 25%.

test.method: Not a test; a QA step before reading any heatmap.
test.measure: Whether the screenshot matches the live page

title: Run a post-purchase survey asking what made them buy and what almost stopped them
hypothesis: If every store asks buyers what almost stopped them from purchasing, then the store gets a direct source of objections to answer in hero copy, FAQs and tests, because buyer-stated objections are more reliable than guessed ones.

signal.check: No post-purchase survey exists on the thank-you page.

risk.note: A survey add; can be removed if unhelpful.

prerequisites: A survey app (KnoCommerce, Okendo, or similar)
steps: Install a post-purchase survey on the thank-you page.
Ask at least: 'What made you purchase today?' and 'What made you almost not purchase today?'
Keep attribution questions like 'how did you hear about us' in a separate survey.
After 2 to 4 weeks or 100+ answers, group responses into themes.
Check whether each theme is answered near the decision on the PDP, cart and checkout.
Re-survey after a fix ships to see whether the theme declines.

test.method: Not a test; a research input that feeds hypotheses.
test.measure: Objection themes and their frequency over time
test.read_point: Every 2 to 4 weeks, and after any related fix ships

title: Run an exit-intent survey to capture reasons from non-buyers
hypothesis: If we ask exiting non-buyers what stopped them or what almost stopped them, then we capture objections a post-purchase survey never can, because post-purchase surveys only hear from people who already bought.

signal.check: The store has a post-purchase survey but no exit survey for non-buyers.

risk.note: A survey add.

prerequisites: Enough traffic for meaningful response volume
steps: Add an exit-intent survey with questions like 'What stopped you from buying?' and 'What's the reason you're exiting the site?'
Group answers into themes: product uncertainty, price, shipping, trust gaps, missing info, comparison needs.
Cross-check themes with recordings and funnel data before writing a hypothesis.

test.method: Not a test; a research input.

title: Bootstrap a one-time customer survey if no post-purchase survey exists yet
hypothesis: If we email customers and VIPs a one-time survey with the same core questions, then we get objection data immediately instead of waiting for the post-purchase survey to accumulate answers, because the store needs research input now, not in a few weeks.

signal.check: No post-purchase survey exists and the store needs research input soon.

risk.note: A one-time email survey.

prerequisites: Customer email list
a form tool (Typeform or similar)
steps: Build a one-time survey with the same core questions as the post-purchase survey.
Email it to customers and VIPs, optionally with an incentive like a prize draw.
Check prize-draw and data-privacy rules in the brand's market before running the incentive.
Use answers only until the post-purchase survey is live and has enough data.

test.method: Not a test; a bootstrap research input.

title: Mine reviews with an LLM, then confirm every theme against the source reviews
hypothesis: If we export reviews, prompt an LLM for objections and unique feedback, and then read the source reviews behind each theme, then the PDP can answer real objections and use verbatim positioning, because the LLM can over-generalise if not checked.

signal.check: The store has 500 or more reviews that have never been mined for themes.

risk.note: A research step.

prerequisites: Review export (CSV) from the review app
steps: Export all reviews to CSV from the review app.
Prompt an LLM for commonalities, tone, buzzwords, friction points, objections and unique feedback.
Read the source reviews behind each claimed theme to confirm it.
Send objections to the FAQ and hero copy; send unique feedback to positioning.
Include at least 3 verbatim reviews behind every theme used.

test.method: Not a test; a research input that feeds copy hypotheses.
test.measure: Number of confirmed objection themes with verbatims

title: Run task-based user tests with 5 to 8 people before a redesign or after an unexplained funnel drop
hypothesis: If we run task-based tests with 5 to 8 people (first impressions, find a product, add to cart, check out), then hidden friction shows up that heatmaps and surveys miss, because these are small qualitative samples aimed at behaviour, not conversion estimates.

signal.check: A redesign is planned, or a funnel drop has no obvious cause, and no user test has been run.

expected_effect.size: unknown; qualitative samples, not conversion estimates

risk.note: A research cost, not a site change.

prerequisites: A user-testing tool or panel (Userbrain or similar)
steps: Recruit 5 to 8 people per task.
First prompt: first impressions on landing.
Real tasks: find a suitable product, add it to cart, check out.
Note missed navigation, misread details, missed info, hesitation and checkout doubts.
Turn any pattern seen in at least 2 testers into a hypothesis.

test.method: Not a test; a qualitative research round.
test.read_point: Before a redesign, or after an unexplained funnel drop

title: Buy from the store's own site every 4 weeks on mobile, desktop and tablet
hypothesis: If someone buys from the store every 4 weeks on every device, then popups, cookie banners and bugs covering the CTA or cart button get caught and repaired quickly, because self-purchase catches what analytics tools can miss.

signal.check: No self-purchase audit has happened in the last 4 weeks.

risk.note: A recurring check, low cost.

steps: Buy from the store on mobile, desktop and tablet.
Ask someone unfamiliar with the site to buy on a phone while you watch.
Look for exit popups or cookie banners covering the PDP CTA or cart button.
Note any bugs found and log them as repairs.
Repeat every 4 weeks and before every test launch.

test.method: Not a test; a recurring manual audit.
test.measure: Number of blockers found per audit

title: Call recent buyers to hear their own words for the product and any checkout friction
hypothesis: If we call recent buyers and ask why they bought, whether checkout was easy, and what words they use for the product, then messaging hypotheses get grounded in real customer language, because survey answers are sometimes too thin to act on.

signal.check: Survey answers on objections or motivations are thin or ambiguous.

risk.note: A research step.

prerequisites: Recent buyer contact list
steps: Pick a small sample of recent flagship-SKU buyers, or a random sample across the catalogue.
Ask why they bought, whether checkout was easy, and what words they use for the product.
Feed the language directly into messaging hypotheses.

test.method: Not a test; a research input.
test.measure: Number of usable phrases and objections gathered
test.read_point: Any time survey data is thin

title: Pick a behaviour tool by the store's daily session volume, not by feature lists
hypothesis: If a low-traffic store defaults to Clarity's free tier before paying for an all-in-one platform, then the store gets heatmaps and recordings without an unnecessary bill, because Hotjar-style platforms price by daily sessions and can cost more than the value they add at low volume.

signal.check: The store pays for an all-in-one behaviour platform while running under a few hundred daily sessions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a cost decision, not a conversion lift

risk.note: A tool decision.

prerequisites: Daily session volume, normal and peak
steps: Check daily sessions, normal and peak.
Under a few hundred daily sessions, default to Clarity's free tier for heatmaps and recordings.
Move to an all-in-one platform only when surveys, interviews or funnels beyond GA4 Explore are worth the added cost.
Confirm current pricing and limits before committing.
Confirm privacy, retention and any feature in active use before migrating tools.

test.method: Not a test; a tool selection decision.

title: Set the behaviour tool review window to the longest representative period
hypothesis: If we set the review window to about 6 months, or 90 days if the tool is newer, then findings reflect normal behaviour rather than a one-off spike, because a big site, merchandising or traffic change makes an older window less representative.

signal.check: A behaviour review uses a default or arbitrary date range.

risk.note: A window setting.

steps: Set the date range to about 6 months, or 90 days if the tool or store is newer.
Re-set the window after a big site, merchandising or traffic change.

test.method: Not a test; a settings step.

title: Use GA4 Explore for funnel building before paying for a separate funnel tool
hypothesis: If we build the purchase funnel in GA4 Explore before buying a dedicated funnel feature, then the store avoids paying twice for the same thing, because GA4 Explore already builds custom funnels once ecommerce tracking is configured.

signal.check: A tool budget includes a funnel feature the store could build in GA4 Explore.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a cost saving, not a conversion lift

risk.note: A tool decision.

prerequisites: GA4 ecommerce tracking configured
steps: Confirm GA4 ecommerce tracking is correctly configured.
Build the funnel in GA4 Explore: product view, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase.
Only add a paid funnel tool if GA4 Explore cannot answer the question.

test.method: Not a test; a tool decision.
test.measure: Whether GA4 Explore covers the funnel need

title: Use competitor and paid-ad landing pages for layout and mood research only
hypothesis: If we study competitor and paid-ad landing pages only for layout and mood, and never copy their text, logos, products or faces, then hypothesis generation gets outside patterns without any legal or ethical risk, because a paid ad being run does not prove the page is profitable.

signal.check: The team is generating hypotheses with no outside pattern research at all.

risk.note: Never copy text, logos, products or faces from a competitor page.

steps: Collect competitor and paid-ad landing pages relevant to the category.
Note layout and mood patterns only.
Keep this research separate from private brand data.
Never copy text, logos, products or faces into the store's own page.

test.method: Not a test; a hypothesis-generation input.

title: Write every hypothesis in the pre-registration form before it enters the backlog
hypothesis: If every hypothesis is written as 'because we observed X, we believe change Y will cause effect Z for segment W, measured by metric M, and we will know it worked if M moves by at least the MDE', then any reader can audit and run the test, because the form forces evidence, a clear change and a measurable outcome.

signal.check: A backlog entry is a vague idea with no evidence, change, effect or metric named.

risk.note: A documentation standard.

prerequisites: At least 2 points of evidence per idea
steps: State the evidence observed.
State the specific change.
State the expected effect and the segment it applies to.
State the primary metric and the minimum detectable effect that counts as a win.

test.method: Not a test; a documentation standard applied before any test is designed.
test.measure: Whether every backlog entry follows the form
test.read_point: Before every backlog entry is accepted

title: Cross-check survey themes against funnel and heatmap data before writing the hypothesis
hypothesis: If a survey theme also shows up as a funnel drop at the matching step and as hunting behaviour in recordings, then the hypothesis has three points of evidence instead of one, because a theme confirmed across sources is far more likely to be real.

signal.check: A survey-derived hypothesis has not been checked against funnel or heatmap data.

risk.note: A cross-check step.

prerequisites: Survey themes
funnel memo
heatmap or recordings
steps: Take a survey-derived theme.
Check whether it shows as a drop at the matching funnel step.
Check whether it shows as hunting behaviour in recordings.
After the fix ships, re-survey to see whether the theme declines.

test.method: Not a test; a cross-check before writing the hypothesis.
test.measure: Number of evidence points per hypothesis

title: Rank the backlog by expected profit, with a ceiling estimate, not by expected lift alone
hypothesis: If the backlog is ranked by probability of winning times expected lift times gross profit per conversion times traffic exposed, minus build cost, then a small lift on a high-value page can rank above a big lift on a low-value page, because a 20% lift on a low-margin, low-traffic page can be worth less than a 5% lift on the hero checkout.

signal.check: The backlog is sorted by expected percentage lift with no profit or traffic weighting.

risk.note: A ranking method.

prerequisites: SKU margin
page traffic by candidate test page
steps: For each idea, estimate probability of winning from evidence, not the idea owner's confidence.
Estimate expected lift, gross profit per conversion and traffic exposed.
Compute expected value and subtract build cost.
Add a ceiling estimate: the most it could be worth if it wins.
Sort the backlog by expected value.

test.method: Not a test; a ranking method applied to the whole backlog.

title: Score PDP, cart and checkout ideas with evidence-gated criteria, never let the idea's owner be the only scorer
hypothesis: If PDP, cart and checkout ideas are scored against evidence-tied criteria (above the fold, noticeable in 5 seconds, high-traffic page, backed by research, build difficulty) by more than one person, then the score reflects the idea's real strength, because a founder or merchandiser scoring their own idea on a 1 to 10 scale tends to inflate it.

signal.check: The idea's own pitcher is the only person scoring it on an ICE-style 1 to 10 scale.

risk.note: A scoring method.

prerequisites: Evidence gate already applied (CRO-020)
steps: List the evidence-tied criteria: above the fold, noticeable within 5 seconds, high-traffic page, backed by heatmap or survey or user test or analytics, build difficulty.
Score each idea against the criteria with more than one scorer.
For a small team still building the habit, ICE (impact, confidence, ease, 1 to 10 each) is acceptable, but never scored by the idea's own owner alone.
Combine the score with expected value (CRO-044) to break ties.

test.method: Not a test; a scoring method.

title: Rank above-the-fold PDP and homepage changes ahead of below-the-fold work by default
hypothesis: If above-the-fold changes (hero, price, CTA) rank ahead of below-the-fold collection filters by default, then testing effort goes where most mobile shoppers decide, because a large share of shoppers reportedly never scroll past the top section on a phone.

signal.check: The backlog ranks below-fold work ahead of above-the-fold changes with no research pointing there.

expected_effect.size: unknown; directional priority, not a stated lift

does_not_apply_when: Research clearly points to a below-fold problem

risk.note: A ranking preference, not a forbidden action.

steps: Default to prioritising above-the-fold changes: hero, price, CTA.
Only prioritise below-the-fold work when research (survey, recording, heatmap) points there.
Do not treat this as a rule that forbids below-fold tests.

test.method: Not a test; a ranking preference.

title: Work page changes in order: clarity, then copy, then offer, then proof, then friction
hypothesis: If page-level work is sequenced clarity first, then copy, then offer, then proof, then friction, then the biggest, cheapest wins ship first, because a bad offer keeps conversion near zero no matter how good the rest is, but the offer is also the hardest thing to fix.

signal.check: Work is picked ad hoc with no sequencing logic.

risk.note: A sequencing rule.

steps: Fix clarity issues first (see clarity-fix idea).
Rework copy next.
Address the offer, even though it is hardest, and do not let it wait indefinitely.
Add or improve proof.
Remove friction last.

test.method: Not a test; a sequencing rule for choosing which class of change to work on.
test.read_point: Whenever choosing what to work on next for a page

title: Ship an obvious clarity fix directly instead of running a test on it
hypothesis: If an unambiguous, research-backed clarity fix ships without a test, then the store gets a quick win without spending weeks proving something obvious, because fixing an unclear page rarely needs a split test to justify it.

signal.check: A clarity fix that both versions cannot plausibly disagree on is sitting in the test backlog instead of shipping.

does_not_apply_when: Both versions are plausibly viable and the better one is unknown (use R52 instead)

risk.note: Ship, then verify with fresh recordings and the funnel step.

prerequisites: Research confirming the fix is unambiguous
steps: Confirm the fix is unambiguous and backed by research, not opinion.
Ship it directly without a test.
Log the change and the reason.
Watch fresh recordings and the funnel step to confirm the fix worked.

test.method: Before-and-after monitoring (weak evidence), not a randomised test.
test.measure: Funnel step rate and recordings after shipping

title: Re-audit the page after every shipped change
hypothesis: If every shipped change is followed by fresh recordings, a re-read of the funnel step and a re-survey, then the next friction point gets found quickly, because fixing one element often exposes another.

signal.check: A change shipped with no plan to re-check it.

risk.note: A monitoring step.

prerequisites: Behaviour tool and survey in place
steps: Watch fresh recordings of the new version.
Re-read the affected funnel step.
Re-survey for the objection the change addressed.

test.method: Not a test; a monitoring step after every ship.
test.measure: Funnel step rate, survey theme frequency

title: Repair defects immediately instead of testing them
hypothesis: If a page error, a broken field, a silent cart wipe, double-firing tracking or a popup covering the CTA is repaired immediately instead of tested, then no shopper is deliberately left on a broken experience, because randomising traffic onto a known defect only proves what is already known.

signal.check: A known defect (page error, broken add to cart, tracking firing twice, cart wipe, a fake-button element, a popup over the CTA) is in the test backlog instead of the repair list.

risk.note: Fixing a known defect carries little downside.

steps: Check whether the current state is objectively defective: errors, rejected valid input, browser failure, double tracking, a blocked CTA, a silent cart wipe, a fake-button element.
If yes, repair it now.
Log the repair so it is never re-proposed as a test hypothesis.
Verify the fix with fresh recordings.

test.method: No test; repair and verify with fresh recordings.
test.measure: Whether the defect is gone in fresh recordings

title: Ship a proven or unambiguous change without a test at a low-order store
hypothesis: If a store under 30 orders a month ships a clarity fix or a proven checkout practice directly, then it avoids running a test it cannot power, because the store cannot reach a meaningful sample in a reasonable time.

signal.check: The store runs under 30 orders a month and a change is stuck in a test backlog it cannot power.

does_not_apply_when: Store runs 30+ orders a month and can reach a planned sample in 2 to 4 weeks

risk.note: Confirm the ship with fresh recordings and funnel step rate.

prerequisites: Monthly order count under 30
steps: Confirm the store runs under 30 orders a month, or the change cannot plausibly hurt.
Ship the change without a test.
Confirm with fresh recordings and the funnel step rate.
Treat any before-and-after shift as weak evidence, not proof.

test.method: Before-and-after monitoring, treated as weak evidence.
test.measure: Funnel step rate before and after

title: Run an A/B test only when both versions are plausibly viable and the sample is reachable in weeks
hypothesis: If a test only runs when both versions could plausibly win and the planned sample is reachable in 2 to 4 weeks, then the team never launches a test that cannot resolve, because most other changes should be a repair or a ship instead.

signal.check: A test is planned where one version obviously helps or hurts, or where the sample would take months.

risk.note: A decision gate.

prerequisites: Weekly eligible traffic on the tested page
steps: Confirm both versions are plausibly viable and the better one is unknown.
Compute the sample size needed (see test-sizing idea).
If reachable in 2 to 4 weeks, run the test.
If not reachable, raise the MDE, move to a higher-traffic page, or ship as a bold change with a later holdout.

test.method: A/B test, sized per P13.

title: Use the order-per-month gate to set test ambition, then compute the real sample size
hypothesis: If test ambition is set by monthly orders (under 30 research only, 30 to 300 one bold test, 300 to 3,000 regular A/B, 3,000 to 20,000 A/B/n and bandits, 20,000+ full programme), then a store never plans a test its traffic cannot support, because the gates map to how many conversions per variant are realistic.

signal.check: A test plan does not state the store's current orders-per-month band.

expected_effect.size: unknown; these are heuristics, always compute the real sample

risk.note: A planning heuristic, not a rule that overrides sample math.

prerequisites: Monthly order count
steps: Compute the store's current orders per month.
Match to a band: under 30 research only; 30 to 300 one bold test at 20%+ MDE; 300 to 3,000 regular A/B at 10 to 20%; 3,000 to 20,000 A/B/n and bandits at 5 to 10%; 20,000+ full programme at 2 to 5%.
Sanity-check against 03's 300,000-sessions gate and 02's $40M-revenue gate.
Always compute the real sample size (see test-sizing idea) rather than relying on the band alone.

test.method: Not a test; a planning gate used before designing any test.

title: Below the testing threshold, run bold changes on the highest-traffic pages instead of many small tests
hypothesis: If a low-volume store runs one bold, research-backed change on its highest-traffic page instead of several small tests on low-traffic pages, then it learns more per month, because one bold homepage test can teach more than many micro-tests on low-traffic category pages.

signal.check: A low-volume store is running several small tests on low-traffic pages at once.

risk.note: Bold changes can plausibly hurt as well as help; keep the ability to revert.

prerequisites: Below the store's testing threshold (R53)
steps: Pick the single highest-traffic page: home, hero product or cart.
Design one bold change backed by qualitative research, aimed at a 10 to 20%+ effect.
Run it alone, not alongside several smaller tests.
Re-test a surprising big winner with a holdout before banking it.

test.method: A single bold A/B test on the highest-traffic page.
test.measure: cvr_overall or the tested step's rate

title: Treat any before-and-after page comparison as biased, not just noisy
hypothesis: If a before-and-after comparison is only used for big structural changes with equal comparable periods, then promos, restocks and seasonality never get mistaken for a page effect, because they confound the change with time exactly like a real page change would.

signal.check: A revenue change is attributed to a page change using a simple before-and-after comparison with no equal comparable period.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a false conclusion rather than creating a lift

risk.note: A reading discipline.

steps: Reserve before-and-after reads for big structural changes where the effect dwarfs noise.
Use equal comparable periods and hold conditions constant (seasonality, promos, weekday mix, traffic-source shifts).
Treat a clear, stable, explainable shift as weak evidence, not proof.
Confirm later with a randomised test where possible.

test.method: Not a test; a reading rule for any non-randomised comparison.
test.read_point: Any time a before-and-after comparison is used, including checkout repairs

title: Do not add test arms below the traffic threshold; run sequential single tests instead
hypothesis: If a store under 3,000 orders a month runs one test after another instead of adding arms, then each test stays properly powered, because A/B/n needs the full per-variant sample for every arm and total traffic scales with the number of arms.

signal.check: A test plan adds 3 or more arms while the store runs under 3,000 orders a month.

risk.note: A test design rule.

prerequisites: Monthly order count
steps: Check monthly orders.
Below 300 to 3,000 orders a month, keep A/B/n to 2 to 3 arms at most, and prefer running tests one after another.
Above 3,000, A/B/n with more arms is routine.

test.method: Not a test; a design rule applied before launching any multi-arm test.

title: Use A/B tests for durable decisions and bandits only for short tactical campaigns
hypothesis: If a durable decision (redesign, pricing logic, navigation, checkout) always runs as an A/B test, and only short regret-minimising campaigns (headlines, seasonal promos, banner creative) use a bandit, then the store gets a clean causal read where it matters and less wasted exposure where it does not, because bandits estimate effects poorly but shift traffic to the winner faster.

signal.check: A bandit is used for a lasting decision, or an A/B test is used for a short seasonal promo with a costly loser.

risk.note: Bandits need sticky bucketing so returning users stay on one arm.

prerequisites: A testing tool that supports bandits
about 3,000+ orders a month for routine use
steps: For a lasting decision, run a standard A/B test.
For a short, regret-costly campaign (headline, seasonal promo, banner), use a bandit like Thompson sampling or UCB.
Ensure sticky bucketing so a returning user stays on one arm.
Reserve routine bandit use for stores at about 3,000+ orders a month.

test.method: A/B test or bandit, chosen by the decision type.
test.read_point: At planned sample, or continuously for a bandit

title: Never run two tests on the same page area, and never two tests on the same PDP, at once
hypothesis: If the test calendar never allows two tests on the same page area or the same PDP at once, then a result never gets confounded by a second change happening at the same time, because the same funnel step being touched twice makes the read unreadable.

signal.check: The test calendar has two tests running on the same page area, or on the same PDP, at the same time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a confounded read rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A scheduling rule.

prerequisites: A shared test calendar
steps: Keep a shared test calendar naming the page and area each test touches.
Before launching, check no other live test touches the same page area.
A homepage test and a cart test can run together since they touch different funnel steps.
Above about 20,000 orders a month, apply false-discovery-rate control for many concurrent tests.

test.method: Not a test; a calendar rule applied before every launch.

title: Size every test from the minimum detectable effect, never from a round conversion number
hypothesis: If every test is sized with n = 16 x p(1-p) / delta squared per variant, then the test has a real chance of detecting the smallest lift worth shipping, because halving the MDE quadruples the needed sample and a guessed sample size can under-power the test.

signal.check: A test brief states a sample size with no MDE calculation behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a sizing method, not a lift

risk.note: A sizing calculation.

prerequisites: Baseline conversion rate for the page and device
steps: Set the MDE to the smallest lift worth shipping in gross profit terms, not the smallest lift possible.
Confirm whether the calculator wants a relative or absolute MDE.
Compute n = 16 x p(1-p) / delta squared per variant at alpha 0.05, power 0.80, two-sided.
Use Evan Miller's calculator or the sample table (see below) as a cross-check.

test.method: Not a test itself; the sizing method for every test.

title: State every sample size as orders per variant, and reject flat magic numbers
hypothesis: If sample size is always stated as orders per variant instead of sessions, clicks, or a flat number like '400 conversions a month', then finance and the founder can track it against the P&L and no one under-powers a test on a borrowed rule of thumb, because a flat number ignores the store's own baseline and MDE.

signal.check: A brief or a vendor quotes a flat conversion number with no baseline or MDE behind it.

expected_effect.size: about 3,830 conversions per variant for a 5% relative lift, about 1,000 for 10%, about 260 for 20%, about 120 for 30%, at 80% power and 95% confidence

risk.note: A reporting standard.

prerequisites: Sample size computed per CRO-059
steps: State the computed sample as orders (conversions) per variant, then multiply by the number of arms for the total.
Reject any magic number like '400 conversions a month' or a flat per-group rule with no MDE behind it.
Use 05's per-variant table for common baselines and MDEs as a sanity check.

test.method: Not a test; a reporting standard.

title: Compute test runtime from arms times sample, divided by weekly traffic on the tested page
hypothesis: If runtime is computed as total sample divided by weekly eligible traffic on the tested page, rounded up to whole weeks, then the team knows before launch whether the test is realistic, because using sitewide sessions instead of page traffic overstates how fast the sample will fill.

signal.check: A runtime estimate uses sitewide sessions instead of traffic on the specific tested page or path.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning calculation, not a lift

risk.note: A planning calculation.

prerequisites: Weekly eligible traffic on the tested page
steps: Multiply the per-variant sample by the number of arms.
Divide by weekly eligible traffic on the tested page or path, not sitewide sessions.
Round up to whole weeks.
If the runtime is unreasonable, raise the MDE, move to a higher-traffic page, switch to a faster micro-conversion primary, or drop to research only.

test.method: Not a test; a runtime planning step.

title: Run every test at least 2 full weeks, covering each weekday twice, and to the planned sample
hypothesis: If every test runs at least 2 full weeks and covers each weekday twice, then a one-day shock like a competitor's sale cannot trigger a wrong kill, because weekday and weekend shoppers convert differently and 2 weeks captures a full cycle of returning visitors.

signal.check: A test is planned to run under 1 week, or for an odd number of days that splits weeks unevenly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a wrong call rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A scheduling rule.

steps: Set the minimum runtime to 2 full weeks.
Plan the end date to cover each weekday twice.
Do not stop early just because significance is hit ahead of schedule.
Also confirm the planned sample was reached, not just the time.

test.method: Not a test; a runtime rule applied to every test.
test.read_point: At test launch and at planned close

title: Default every test to two-tailed unless a documented reason justifies one-tailed
hypothesis: If every brief defaults to a two-tailed test, then downside is never hidden by a shortcut to faster significance, because a one-tailed test only checks one direction and standard sample tables assume two-sided testing.

signal.check: A brief uses a one-tailed test with no documented reason.

risk.note: A design rule.

steps: Default every brief to two-tailed.
Only use one-tailed when a negative result would trigger the same action as a null result (keep control either way), documented before launch.
Recompute the sample size for the chosen tail, since tables differ.

test.method: Not a test; a design rule.

title: Remove retention traffic from the test population, or isolate it on a cold-only landing page
hypothesis: If email and other retention traffic is excluded or isolated from a page test, then the result reflects the intended audience, because Klaviyo sends and other retention traffic can spike conversion and split-test tools can fork that traffic into the test too.

signal.check: A test runs on a page that receives both paid and owned (email, SMS) traffic with no exclusion plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a contaminated read rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: Excluding email traffic is reversible, but requires coordination with the retention team.

prerequisites: Ability to exclude retention traffic in Klaviyo or the ad platform
steps: Identify whether the tested page receives retention (email, SMS) traffic.
Exclude that traffic from the test, or send tests to custom landing pages that only receive cold Meta traffic.
Alternatively, fork traffic at the ad-set or campaign level so only one arm's traffic reaches each page.
Account for multi-click journeys: some buyers click more than once and may see both variants without sticky bucketing.

test.method: Not a test on its own; a contamination-control step applied before launching a paid-traffic test.
test.measure: Share of retention traffic in the test population
test.read_point: Before launch, and checked during the test

title: Randomise by user with sticky bucketing so returning visitors always see the same arm
hypothesis: If randomisation is done at the user level with sticky bucketing, then a returning visitor never sees both variants, because the randomisation unit must stay consistent for the result to mean anything.

signal.check: A testing tool's randomisation unit or sticky bucketing setting has not been confirmed.

risk.note: A configuration check.

prerequisites: Testing tool access
steps: Confirm the randomisation unit is the user, not the session or page view.
Confirm sticky bucketing is on so a returning user sees the same arm every time.
Confirm this for both A/B tests and bandits.

test.method: Not a test; a configuration check before launch.

title: Pick a stopping rule before launch and never look between planned looks
hypothesis: If a fixed-horizon or a validated sequential engine is chosen before launch and the stopping rule is followed exactly, then the reported p-value stays valid, because peeking daily and stopping at the first significant result inflates the false-positive rate far above 5%.

signal.check: A team checks a live test daily and plans to stop as soon as it looks significant.

expected_effect.size: peeking daily and stopping at the first p<0.05 can turn a nominal 5% false-positive rate into 26.1% in the worst case

risk.note: A peeked result cannot be un-peeked; the fix is prevention, not correction after the fact.

prerequisites: Testing tool with a stated stats engine
steps: Before launch, choose fixed horizon (look once at the planned sample) or a validated sequential engine (mSPRT, GAVI, group sequential with alpha spending).
Write the chosen method and its exact stopping rule into the brief.
Under fixed horizon, do not act on any interim read.
Under a sequential engine, only its own rule may stop the test.

test.method: Not a test; a stopping-rule discipline applied to every test.
test.measure: Whether the test was stopped per its stated rule
test.read_point: At every planned look, and at close

title: Treat an unstated Bayesian prior as a peeked frequentist test
hypothesis: If we confirm the prior and the optional-stopping protection of any Bayesian testing tool before trusting it, then a flat-prior tool being watched daily does not get treated as immune to peeking, because most commercial Bayesian tools are close to frequentist with less transparency.

signal.check: A Bayesian testing tool (VWO SmartStats, AB Tasty, Eppo, or similar) is used with no stated prior or stopping protection.

expected_effect.size: one simulation found peeking every 100 observations and stopping a Bayesian test at P>0.95 gives about an 80% false-positive rate

risk.note: Same caution as peeking: prevention, not correction after the fact.

prerequisites: Vendor documentation for the testing tool's stats engine
steps: Check the vendor docs for the tool's prior and whether its stopping threshold is protected against optional stopping.
If the prior cannot be stated, treat the tool's result like a peeked frequentist test.
Size the test as fixed horizon in that case.

test.method: Not a test; a vendor-verification step.
test.read_point: Before adopting or trusting any Bayesian testing tool

title: Choose the stats engine before writing the test brief, based on how well traffic can be forecast
hypothesis: If the stats engine is chosen based on whether the expected sample can be forecast well, then the test uses the most powerful method available without inviting peeking risk, because a fixed horizon is more powerful when traffic is stable and an always-valid method protects against daily watching when it is not.

signal.check: A brief is written with no named stats engine.

risk.note: A planning decision.

prerequisites: Traffic stability known
vendor engine confirmed
steps: If traffic and baseline are stable and can be estimated well, choose fixed horizon or group sequential with alpha spending.
If not, or if stakeholders will watch daily, choose an always-valid method (mSPRT, GAVI, corrected alpha), accepting wider intervals.
Confirm the tool's current engine in vendor docs before committing.
Run an A/A test first if this is a new tool or a new programme.

test.method: Not a test; an engine-selection step before writing the brief.

title: Require statistical power, not just significance, before trusting a testing tool's verdict
hypothesis: If every test is sized for power before launch instead of relying on a tool's 'significant' label, then a result that repeats is far more likely, because significance without power is like flipping 3 coins and getting 2 heads.

signal.check: A testing tool reports 'significant' with no sample-size calculation behind the test.

risk.note: A discipline check.

prerequisites: Weekly order volume for the tested page
steps: Size the test yourself from the page's weekly order volume before launch (see test-sizing idea).
Do not accept a tool's 'significant' label as sufficient on its own.
Confirm the planned sample was reached before trusting the verdict.

test.method: Not a test; a discipline check applied to every readout.

title: Check sample ratio mismatch at launch and at every planned look
hypothesis: If a chi-square goodness-of-fit check on users runs at launch and every planned look, then a broken randomisation gets caught before the result is trusted, because about 6% of large-platform experiments show a sample ratio mismatch and even a 50.3/49.7 split can flag one on a large sample.

signal.check: A live or closed test has never had an SRM check run on it.

expected_effect.size: flag at p < 0.001; about 6% of experiments show SRM at large platforms

risk.note: An SRM-flagged test cannot be trusted retroactively; the cause must be found before any result is used.

prerequisites: User-level assignment data from the testing tool
steps: Run a chi-square goodness-of-fit check on users, not page views, at launch and at each planned look.
Flag anything at p < 0.001.
If flagged, stop trusting the result until the cause (bots, redirects, tracking, browser-specific failures) is found.

test.method: Not a test; a validity check applied to every test.
test.read_point: At launch and every planned look

title: QA every test 2 to 3 times on real devices and confirm tracking fires in both arms before launch
hypothesis: If every test is QA'd 2 to 3 times on real devices and tracking is confirmed in both arms before launch, then a bug never makes a winner look like a loser, because an untested variant can silently break add to cart or tracking.

signal.check: A test is about to launch with no documented QA pass on real devices.

risk.note: A QA step before launch.

prerequisites: Access to test devices, browsers and connection speeds
steps: QA both arms 2 to 3 times on real devices, mobile first, on different browsers and connection speeds.
Check add to cart, cart and checkout start work in both arms.
Confirm the tool's conversion count matches the store backend for a short window.
If tracking breaks mid-test, invalidate the read and restart.

test.method: Not a test; a launch QA checklist.
test.read_point: Before launch, and spot-checked during the test

title: Check for flicker on a slow mobile connection before trusting a client-side test
hypothesis: If flicker is checked on a slow mobile connection before trusting a client-side test, then an inflated effect from the control briefly flashing before the variant loads gets caught, because flicker both hurts the experience and can bias the read.

signal.check: A client-side test has not been checked for flicker on a slow mobile connection.

expected_effect.size: anti-flicker snippets hide the page for up to 3 to 4 seconds by default

risk.note: If flicker is severe, move to server-side testing or Shopify Rollouts.

prerequisites: Access to test on a throttled mobile connection
steps: Load the variant on a simulated slow mobile connection.
Check whether the original renders before the variant swaps in.
If flicker is present, prefer server-side testing or Shopify Rollouts for speed-sensitive paths.
If accepting an anti-flicker snippet, record the hidden-page duration as a cost.

test.method: Not a test; a QA check before trusting a client-side test.

title: Check the marketing calendar for promo or holiday overlap before launching a test
hypothesis: If the marketing calendar is checked before every test window, then a promotion or holiday never silently confounds the result, because a sale inside the window moves orders exactly like a page change would.

signal.check: A test window has not been checked against the marketing calendar for promos or holidays.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a confound rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A scheduling check.

prerequisites: Marketing calendar for the test window
steps: Check the marketing calendar for promos, launches and holidays inside the planned window.
Filter bots from the test population.
If a sale or holiday falls inside the window, move the dates.
If overlap cannot be avoided, note the confound in the record and consider a re-run.

test.method: Not a test; a pre-launch check.

title: Pre-register device and traffic segments before reading any result, and correct for multiple comparisons
hypothesis: If mobile vs desktop and cold-paid vs returning are pre-registered before the test, and Bonferroni or FDR correction is applied for multiple metrics, then a blended win never hides a mobile loss and slicing after the fact never manufactures a false winner, because reading more metrics and segments inflates the error rate.

signal.check: A readout slices by device or segment after the fact with no pre-registration, or reads several metrics with no correction.

expected_effect.size: reading 1 metric carries about 5% error, 2 about 10%, 3 about 14%, at alpha 0.05 each

risk.note: A design and reading discipline.

steps: Pre-register device, paid vs organic, and new vs returning segments before launch.
Decide on the pre-declared overall metric first.
Apply Bonferroni or FDR correction when reading multiple metrics.
Treat any post-hoc slice as a new hypothesis to test, not a proven finding.

test.method: Not a test; a pre-registration and reading rule.

title: Never kill or call a test on the strength of one good or bad day
hypothesis: If a test is never killed or called based on a single day's numbers, then a noisy early swing does not lead to a wrong decision, because early cumulative deltas are the noisiest point in the whole test.

signal.check: Someone proposes stopping a test after one unusually good or bad day.

risk.note: A reading discipline.

steps: Wait for the planned sample and runtime before making any call.
If a single day looks extreme, note it but do not act on it alone.
Only call the test once the stopping rule (fixed horizon or sequential) says to.

test.method: Not a test; a reading discipline applied to every test.
test.read_point: Any day the numbers look extreme

title: Apply Twyman's law: audit any surprising win before celebrating it
hypothesis: If any lift over about 50% is treated as a likely bug rather than a discovery, then the team avoids banking revenue from an instrumentation error, SRM, contamination or a small-sample winner's curse, because realistic lifts are 1 to 5% on mature pages and 10 to 20%+ on unoptimised ones.

signal.check: A test or a case study reports a lift over about 50%, or in the hundreds of percent, with no validity audit run.

expected_effect.size: realistic lifts: 1 to 5% mature pages, 10 to 20%+ unoptimised; 50%+ is suspect

risk.note: A false large win, once shipped and believed, is costly to unwind.

steps: Compare the reported lift against the realistic range for the page's maturity.
If it is far above realistic, run the full validity audit (SRM, tracking, bots, promo overlap, stopping rule, segment count).
Treat a small-sample early-stopped winner as inflated by the winner's curse.
Never treat a case study without baseline, sample, runtime and validity checks as more than hypothesis material.

test.method: Validity audit (see P16-based idea), not a new test.
test.measure: Audit outcome: pass, fail, or hypothesis-only
test.read_point: Any surprising result, before it is banked or shipped

title: Check novelty and primacy with a daily plot before judging a result on the average
hypothesis: If the daily effect is plotted and first-exposure is compared with repeat-exposure, then a temporary novelty bump or a primacy dip gets judged on the stable period instead of the noisy early days, because most suspected novelty effects turn out to be artifacts of noisy early cumulative deltas.

signal.check: A test with returning traffic or a visible design change is read only on its cumulative average, with no daily plot.

risk.note: A reading step.

prerequisites: Daily-level test data
steps: Plot the daily effect across the test period.
Compare first-exposure with repeat-exposure conversion.
Judge the result on the stable period, not the early days.
Do not treat any single threshold as proof of a real novelty effect either way.

test.method: Not a test; a reading step applied at close.
test.read_point: At every test close with returning traffic or a visible design change

title: Run an A/A test whenever starting a new testing programme or switching tools
hypothesis: If an A/A test runs when a new testing tool or programme starts, then a broken platform gets caught before it corrupts every future test, because a significant difference between two identical experiences means the platform itself is faulty.

signal.check: A new testing tool or programme has never had an A/A test run on it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this validates the platform rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: An A/A test costs traffic but carries no site risk.

prerequisites: A testing tool set up
steps: Set up two identical arms with the same experience.
Run the A/A test long enough to reach a meaningful sample.
If a significant difference appears, fix the platform before trusting any future test.
Repeat whenever the tool or its configuration changes materially.

test.method: A/A test.

title: Decide against the confidence interval and business value, not against p < 0.05 alone
hypothesis: If every result is read against its confidence interval, the MDE and incremental gross profit rather than a single p-value, then a marginally significant result never gets mistaken for a sure thing, because roughly 1 in 5 significant wins can still be a false positive when only 10% of ideas are truly effective.

signal.check: A readout reports only 'significant' or 'not significant' with no confidence interval or business-value comparison.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this improves decision quality rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A reading standard.

prerequisites: Confidence interval from the testing tool
steps: Report the effect with its confidence interval, per arm, with sample and dates.
Compare the interval with the MDE, incremental gross profit, build cost and guardrails.
Decide ship, kill or inconclusive from that comparison, not from the p-value alone.
