test.method: Not a test; a reading standard applied at every close.
test.measure: Confidence interval versus MDE and guardrails

title: Treat a fully powered inconclusive test as a real result, not a failure to extend
hypothesis: If a fully powered inconclusive test is recorded as 'effect smaller than the MDE' and closed, then the team stops burning traffic chasing significance that will not appear, because extending a test after it is powered is the same as peeking.

signal.check: A test reached its planned sample with no clear winner and someone proposes running it longer.

risk.note: A decision rule.

steps: Confirm the test reached its planned sample.
If no clear winner, record it as 'effect smaller than the MDE'.
Ship neither version, or the cheaper and simpler one.
Do not extend the test to chase significance.

test.method: Not a test; a closing decision rule.
test.read_point: At planned sample, if no clear winner

title: Replicate or hold out a surprising large win before banking its revenue
hypothesis: If a surprising or unusually large win is replicated or held out before being counted, then the store avoids booking revenue that a bug or a chance result never actually delivered, because both the team's own surprise and an above-realistic lift size are warning signs.

signal.check: A win is above the realistic lift band or was not expected by the team, and it has not been replicated or held out.

risk.note: A verification step before crediting revenue.

prerequisites: Ability to run a follow-up test or holdout
steps: Flag any win above R77's realistic band, or any win the team did not expect.
Run a replication test, or hold out a small share of traffic from the winner.
Only credit the revenue once replicated or the holdout confirms it.

test.method: Replication A/B test or a small holdout.
test.measure: cvr_overall or the primary metric on replication
test.read_point: After the replication or holdout reaches its planned sample

title: Check the mobile-only and desktop-only result before shipping any win
hypothesis: If the mobile and desktop results are checked separately before shipping, then a blended win never hides a mobile loss, because a mobile-first store shipping a desktop-only lift gets little or no benefit.

signal.check: A test result is reported only as a blended number with no device split shown before shipping.

risk.note: A reading check.

prerequisites: Pre-registered device segments
steps: Read the mobile and desktop results separately using the pre-registered segments.
If they move in opposite directions, do not ship blind; investigate before deciding.
On a mobile-first store, do not ship a desktop-only lift.

test.method: Not a test; a reading check before shipping.
test.read_point: At every test close, before shipping

title: Run an LTV and returns check before scaling any angle-driven or claim-driven win
hypothesis: If returns, chargebacks, repeat rate and 365-day LTV are checked by acquisition angle before scaling a winning claim or urgency angle, then the store avoids scaling a page that raises short-term conversion while destroying long-term profit, because over-claiming can lift front-end conversion and quietly raise returns.

signal.check: A win driven by a claim, an urgency angle or a new mechanism is about to be scaled with no LTV or returns check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this prevents a hidden LTV loss rather than creating a gain

risk.note: Pausing to check is low risk; scaling without checking is the risky path.

prerequisites: Returns, chargebacks and LTV data segmented by acquisition angle
steps: Segment returns, chargebacks, repeat rate and 365-day LTV by the acquisition angle behind the win.
Compare against the store's baseline for those metrics.
Only scale spend behind the angle if the guardrails hold.
If they do not hold, treat it as a short-term win with a long-term cost and reconsider.

test.method: Not a test; a guardrail check before scaling spend.
test.measure: Returns, chargebacks, repeat rate and LTV by angle
test.read_point: Before scaling spend behind any winning angle

title: Keep a live-winner register and check quarterly that shipped winners are still live
hypothesis: If every shipped winner is logged in a register and checked at least quarterly, then a theme update or a team change never silently overwrites a proven win, because a win that sticks compounds, but only if someone is watching for it to be undone.

signal.check: No live-winner register exists, or it has not been checked since the last theme, app or team change.

risk.note: A record-keeping habit.

prerequisites: A shared registry or spreadsheet
steps: Log every shipped winner with its ship date in a live-winner register.
Check the register after every theme change, app change or team change.
Restore any winner found to have been overwritten.
Review the full register at least quarterly.

test.method: Not a test; a recurring audit of shipped winners.
test.measure: Number of winners still live versus overwritten
test.read_point: Quarterly, and after every theme, app or team change

title: Set founder expectations at a 10 to 20 percent win rate for PDP, cart and checkout tests
hypothesis: If the founder is told to expect 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 PDP, cart or checkout tests to beat control, then a low win rate does not get mistaken for programme failure, because ecommerce-agency win-rate figures sit far below tech-platform case-study numbers.

signal.check: A founder expects most tests to win, or an agency promises a win rate above 30 to 35% with no stated definition.

expected_effect.size: about 10 to 20% of well-run tests produce a significant winner

risk.note: An expectation-setting conversation.

steps: State the realistic win-rate anchor (10 to 20%) before the programme starts.
Report any win rate with its definition (significant winner per test, decisive rate, or raw), never bare.
Treat any programme claiming above 35% as needing an audit of its definition and stopping rules.
Feed losses back into the next hypothesis instead of treating them as wasted effort.

test.method: Not a test; an expectation-setting and reporting rule.
test.measure: Win rate with its stated definition

title: Keep one experiment log for every test, repair and holdout
hypothesis: If tests, repairs and holdouts all live in one log with hypothesis, method, result and decision, then a loser never gets re-run and a surprising winner gets flagged for replication, because institutional memory is what prevents a programme from fooling itself.

signal.check: Tests, repairs and holdouts are recorded in separate places or not recorded at all.

risk.note: A record-keeping build.

prerequisites: A shared spreadsheet or database
steps: Create one log covering tests, repairs, holdouts and causal analyses.
Record id, date, owner, status, type, page, hypothesis, evidence, metrics, sample, dates, validity checks, result, decision and learning for each entry.
Check the log before proposing any new hypothesis to avoid re-running a loser.
Flag surprising winners in the log for replication.

test.method: Not a test; a record-keeping system used for every future test.
test.read_point: Ongoing, updated at every test event

title: Report programme value from a holdout, never as the sum of individual test lifts
hypothesis: If programme value is reported from a holdout rather than added up from individual test lifts, then the reported number reflects reality, because interaction effects, cumulative drift and attribution confusion make summed lifts unreliable after enough changes ship.

signal.check: A programme report adds up individual test lift percentages to claim overall improvement.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this corrects an overstatement rather than creating a lift

risk.note: A reporting correction.

prerequisites: A programme holdout (see CRO-089)
steps: Stop adding individual shipped-test lift percentages to claim a cumulative improvement.
Report programme value only from a holdout comparison.
Explain the reason: interaction effects, cumulative drift and attribution confusion.

test.method: Not a test; a reporting correction backed by a programme holdout.
test.measure: Net lift from the holdout versus the summed-lift claim

title: Re-verify every shipped change with fresh recordings, funnel step rate and a re-survey
hypothesis: If every ship is followed by fresh recordings, a re-read of the funnel step, and a re-survey for the addressed objection, then the team confirms the fix actually worked instead of assuming it did, because a shipped change can fail silently.

signal.check: A shipped change has no scheduled post-ship verification.

risk.note: A verification step.

prerequisites: Behaviour tool and survey in place
steps: Watch fresh recordings of the shipped version.
Re-read the funnel step the change targeted.
Re-survey for the objection the change addressed and see whether it declines.

test.method: Not a test; a verification step after every ship.
test.measure: Funnel step rate and survey theme frequency after the ship

title: Match the measurement design to the exact question being asked
hypothesis: If the measurement design is picked to match the exact question (A/B test for 'did this test win', feature holdout for 'does this feature add revenue', programme holdout for 'has the programme created value', channel holdout for 'does this channel drive incremental revenue'), then the team never uses the wrong tool for the question, because each design answers a different kind of question.

signal.check: A measurement question is being answered with the wrong design, such as crediting a channel with all attributed conversions instead of running a holdout.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this improves decision quality rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A routing decision.

steps: State the exact question being asked.
Route 'did this test win' to an A/B test.
Route 'does this feature add net revenue' to a feature holdout.
Route 'has the whole programme created value' to a programme holdout.
Route channel or ad incrementality questions to 11-ADC's holdout designs.
Route 'we cannot randomise' questions to a specialist causal method in 06-MEA.
Document the question, method, result and decision in the shared log.

test.method: Not a test; a routing decision that picks the right design.

title: Run a persistent programme holdout to prove the CRO programme's net value
hypothesis: If a small, stable share of traffic is held out from every shipped winner for a fixed period, then the store gets a real net-lift number for the whole programme, because comparing the holdout against everyone else avoids the errors of summing individual test lifts.

signal.check: The store runs a CRO programme with no persistent holdout measuring its cumulative value.

expected_effect.size: one illustration uses 5% holdout, 90 days, comparing 2.5% versus 2.9% conversion (about +16% relative)

does_not_apply_when: Under about 100,000 monthly visitors, where the holdout may not detect the effect; use a longer holdout instead

risk.note: Apply repairs, accessibility and policy fixes to everyone; never withhold those from the holdout.

prerequisites: User-level randomisation available
monthly visitors and logged-in share known
steps: Compute whether the chosen holdout share and period can detect a meaningful effect.
Randomly assign the holdout share to see the site as it was before the programme, sticky by user.
Give everyone else every shipped winner.
Apply repairs, accessibility, policy and major usability fixes to both groups.
Keep assignment stable for the chosen period.
At the end, compare conversion rate and RPV with confidence intervals and report the net lift.

test.method: Persistent programme holdout.
test.measure: cvr_overall and other:rpv, holdout versus exposed group
test.read_point: At the end of the chosen holdout period

title: Measure a popup or recommendation module with a feature holdout, not its own engagement metric
hypothesis: If a popup or recommendation module is measured by a holdout group that never sees it, tracked through to purchase on RPV, then the store learns its true net effect, because opt-in or click counts can rise while purchases fall.

signal.check: A popup, recommendation module, personalisation layer or cart-recovery flow is judged only by its own opt-in, click or open rate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the value could go either way, which is the point of the holdout

risk.note: Expose everyone or remove the feature to end the holdout.

prerequisites: Ability to randomly withhold the feature from a group
steps: Define RPV as the decision metric, with conversion rate, AOV, opt-in rate as support.
Randomly hold out a group that never sees the feature, sticky by user.
Tag and track both groups through to purchase, and to repeat purchase if relevant.
Run long enough to capture delayed purchases.
Read trade-offs: more opt-ins but fewer purchases, or more clicks but no bigger baskets.
Decide to keep, rework or remove the feature based on the pre-declared overall metric.

test.method: Feature holdout.
test.read_point: After enough time to capture delayed purchases

title: Check the traffic gate before choosing a holdout design
hypothesis: If detectability is computed before choosing a user-level, geo or switchback holdout, then a store under about 100,000 monthly visitors uses a longer holdout or a causal method instead of a design it cannot power, because the traffic gate for holdouts is rough guidance, not a hard rule.

signal.check: A holdout design is chosen with no detectability calculation for the store's actual traffic.

risk.note: A planning check.

prerequisites: Monthly visitor count
steps: Check monthly visitors against the rough 100,000 gate for holdout designs.
Below the gate, use a longer holdout period or a stated-assumption causal method instead.
Above it, compute detectability for the specific design before committing.

test.method: Not a test; a planning check before designing a holdout.

title: State and challenge the identifying assumption before trusting any causal method's output
hypothesis: If the identifying assumption behind a causal method (parallel trends, a valid threshold, no unobserved confounding, pre-period similarity) is stated and challenged before its output is trusted, then the store avoids treating a shaky analysis as proof, because these methods substitute for randomisation and each has a specific failure mode.

signal.check: A causal analysis (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, propensity matching, synthetic control) is used with no stated assumption.

risk.note: These are specialist methods; route to a measurement specialist rather than running them without expertise.

prerequisites: A specialist who can implement and evaluate the method
steps: Identify which causal method the question requires.
State its identifying assumption before trusting the output.
Challenge the assumption with available data (for example, matched-market correlation for synthetic control).
Route implementation to a measurement specialist in 06-MEA or 11-ADC.

test.method: Specialist causal analysis (not run inside this playbook's own scope).
test.measure: Stated assumption and its validity check

title: Judge cart-recovery flows against a holdout, not by discount rate alone
hypothesis: If cart-recovery email and SMS flows are judged against a holdout group instead of by how many discounts they send, then the store learns the flow's real incremental value, because frequent discounts can train shoppers to abandon on purpose.

signal.check: A cart-recovery flow's success is measured only by recovered-order count or discount redemption, with no holdout comparison.

risk.note: A measurement change to an existing flow, built in 14-EML.

prerequisites: A cart-recovery flow already live
ability to hold out a comparison group
steps: Hold out a comparison group from the cart-recovery flow.
Compare recovered-order rate between the flow group and the holdout.
Check whether discounts are the only lever, and test non-discount messages too.
Treat the timing framework (first contact within 1 hour, escalation over 72 hours) as a hypothesis to test, not a fixed rule.

test.method: Holdout comparison on the existing cart-recovery flow.
test.read_point: After enough abandoned carts pass through both groups

title: Design the homepage to orient and route shoppers fast, not to convert them directly
hypothesis: If the homepage's job is set as routing to the right products fast and building credibility, with one clear conversion offer, then hero clarity and navigation get fixed instead of chasing a homepage 'conversion rate' that was never the page's job, because the homepage rarely converts directly.

signal.check: The homepage passes a 3-second test poorly, or shows several competing offers instead of one.

expected_effect.size: one case reports a curated set (versus broad assortment) improved add to cart 6.07% and CTR 10.4%; bestsellers for new visitors reported +23.01% CTR; personalised recommendations reported +136% CTR

risk.note: A layout and offer change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Share of sessions starting on the homepage known
steps: Check what share of sessions even start on the homepage.
Show the hero to someone unfamiliar with the brand for 3 seconds and check they can say who, what, why.
Keep navigation simple with clear category entry points and a curated selection.
Reduce to one clear conversion offer with a concrete incentive.
Test bestsellers instead of static featured products for new visitors.

test.method: A/B test on the homepage hero, curation or merchandising.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and CTR to product pages

title: Rebuild the mega menu as a guide with bestsellers and proof at the top
hypothesis: If the mega menu puts a bestsellers carousel, icons and social proof at the top and moves non-money links to the bottom, then new visitors find what they want faster, because new visitors open the menu to see what is on offer, not to find the contact page.

signal.check: Recordings show new visitors opening the menu, and the top of the menu shows contact, reviews or FAQ links instead of products.

risk.note: A navigation change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Recordings of menu use
steps: Watch recordings of new visitors opening the mega menu.
Put a bestsellers carousel, icons and some social proof at the top.
Move non-money links (contact, reviews, FAQs) to the bottom.
Use customer words, not jargon, and do not sort alphabetically.
Keep options to about 6 or fewer at the top level.
Keep the menu icon familiar; avoid a quirky icon or hidden control on mobile.

test.method: A/B test on the new menu structure.

title: Decide whether a collection page is for browsing, deciding or buying before designing it
hypothesis: If a collection page's job (browsing, deciding or buying) is decided from traffic and recordings before design, then the right controls get added, because an Add to Cart button on a browsing-focused page can create decision conflict, while a repeat-buy consumable category might convert better with add-to-cart on the grid.

signal.check: Every collection page uses the same design regardless of category or traffic type.

expected_effect.size: one case (consumables, returning traffic) reports a combined test result of about $30,000 a month with labels combined; no isolated figure

does_not_apply_when: First-time browsing traffic on a non-consumable category

risk.note: A layout change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Traffic mix and recordings for the collection page
steps: Check traffic mix (new vs returning) and recordings for the collection page.
Decide whether the page's job is browsing, deciding or buying.
On a browsing page, avoid Add to Cart buttons that create decision conflict.
For repeat-buy consumables with returning traffic, test price on the card plus add to cart from the grid.
Read new versus returning traffic separately in the result.

test.method: A/B test: add-to-cart-from-grid versus standard grid, segmented by new versus returning traffic.

title: Redesign the mobile collection grid so products show above the fold in the thumb zone
hypothesis: If the mobile collection page shows a 2x2 grid with at least 4 products above the fold and keeps controls in the thumb zone, then shoppers see products immediately instead of a hero banner, because a hero or text block hiding products means starting the page over mentally.

signal.check: Opening a collection page on a phone shows a hero banner or text block instead of products above the fold.

risk.note: A layout change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Mobile device for testing
steps: Open the collection page on a phone.
Cap the hero banner to 30 to 40% of the first view or less.
Show at least a 2x2 grid, 4 products visible above the fold.
Add a sticky bottom filter bar or floating filter pill.
Set tap targets to at least 44px with whitespace.
Label only a few products (bestseller, new, low in stock, trending), and only with real data.

test.method: A/B test on mobile collection layout.

title: Keep promo messaging consistent from collection page to PDP
hypothesis: If a promo shown on the collection page is reinforced on the PDP instead of vanishing, then add-to-cart becomes more likely, because a shopper who loses sight of the promo they came for may hesitate or leave.

signal.check: A promo message appears on the collection page but not on the linked PDPs.

risk.note: A copy consistency fix.

steps: List every live promo shown on collection pages.
Check whether each linked PDP repeats the same promo message.
Add the missing promo reinforcement to any PDP that drops it.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test if traffic allows.

title: Show only real, data-backed scarcity and back-in-stock labels
hypothesis: If a 'low in stock' or back-in-stock label only appears when the stock number is genuinely accurate, then the store can test whether it lifts add to cart without risking the trust cost of a fake or stale scarcity claim.

signal.check: Stock levels are accurate and available, but no low-stock or back-in-stock signal is shown, or a signal is shown that is not backed by real data.

does_not_apply_when: Stock data is not accurate or not available in real time

risk.note: A fake or stale scarcity claim damages trust; only show it when the number is true.

prerequisites: Live, accurate stock level data
steps: Confirm live stock data is accurate for the SKUs in question.
Add a real 'low in stock' label or a back-in-stock notice or waitlist only where the data supports it.
Never invent or round a stock number for effect.
Test whether it lifts add to cart without hurting trust.

test.method: A/B test: real stock label present versus absent.

title: Answer 4 questions above the fold on the PDP: what is it, why this one, why now, why trust you
hypothesis: If the PDP hero answers what it is, why this one, why now and why trust you, ordered value proposition then proof then price then CTA, then a phone shopper gets everything needed to decide without scrolling, because a generic title and no proof or urgency give no reason to choose.

signal.check: The PDP hero has a generic title, no unique-mechanism statement, no urgency and no proof visible on a phone.

risk.note: A hero redesign, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Research on the store's top objections and unique mechanism
steps: Open the PDP on a phone.
Rewrite the hero to answer what is it, why this one, why now, why trust you.
Order elements by persuasive weight: value proposition, proof, price, CTA.
Move SKU details, size and quantity pickers out of the hero, into cart or a sensible default.
Add a scroll cue so the page does not look finished at the fold.

test.method: A/B test on the PDP hero.

title: Put reviews, savings, sticky add-to-cart and a selling gallery next to the buy box
hypothesis: If reviews and stars move higher, savings are visible, add to cart is sticky, and the gallery sells with benefits and UGC instead of only product shots, then purchase drivers sit exactly where the shopper is deciding, because a combined set of these changes reported a large PDP revenue gain.

signal.check: The PDP buy box shows no reviews, no visible savings, a non-sticky add-to-cart, or a gallery of dots and product-only shots.

expected_effect.size: one combined case (5 changes together) reports nearly $40,000 a month and +$0.50 per paid PDP visitor; no isolated figure per change

risk.note: A layout change, easy to revert. Do not credit any single change with the combined result.

steps: Move reviews and star rating higher on the page.
Make any active savings visible near the price.
Make add to cart sticky as the shopper scrolls.
Switch gallery navigation to thumbnails instead of dots.
Use the gallery as a mini landing page: benefits, testimonials, UGC, video, guarantee.
Un-collapse the money-back guarantee next to the CTA, especially for an older audience.

test.method: A/B test, ideally isolating each change if traffic allows; otherwise test the bundle and treat individual attribution as unproven.

title: Make price, shipping cost, returns and delivery time easy to find with consistent currency
hypothesis: If price, shipping, returns and a realistic delivery estimate are all visible without clicking, with consistent currency and origin cues, then a shopper never hits an unexpected surprise, because a mismatched currency note or an inconsistent delivery time reads as a warning sign, not a detail.

signal.check: Shipping cost, returns policy or delivery time require an extra click to find, or currency notes do not match the displayed price.

risk.note: A transparency fix.

steps: Audit the PDP for price, shipping, returns and delivery time visibility without a click.
Check for a mismatched currency note (for example a dollar shipping note on a pound price).
Check review dates are not suspiciously clustered.
Fix any inconsistency found.

test.method: Ship as a repair.

title: Build review volume below about 100 reviews, then shift to relevance and media-first sorting
hypothesis: If a store under about 100 reviews focuses on getting more reviews, and a store above it focuses on relevance and media-first sorting, then proof matches the store's actual maturity, because going from 0 to about 100 reviews reportedly doubled conversion in one store's own data, with diminishing returns after that.

signal.check: Review count and media-review share have not been checked against this threshold before planning proof work.

expected_effect.size: 0 to about 100 reviews roughly doubled conversion in one store's own 2019 to 2020 data; beyond that, the source calls it immeasurable

risk.note: Only incentivise photo reviews where legal; check local rules first.

prerequisites: Review count and media-review share
steps: Check current review count and media-review share.
Below about 100 reviews, prioritise getting more, including image and video reviews.
Above about 100, sort media-first and prioritise 5 hyper-relevant reviews over a generic wall.
Show a mix of 4 and 5 stars rather than a wall of 5.0.
If incentivising photo reviews, check local rules and only reward submitting a review, not a rating.

test.method: A/B test on review sorting or display, or a repair (adding review collection) below 100 reviews.
test.read_point: At planned sample, or ongoing for volume-building

title: Remove generic security seals and test specific policy and proof statements next to the CTA instead
hypothesis: If generic footer security seals are removed and replaced with a specific policy or proof statement (returns, guarantee, customer count, press mention) beside the CTA, then trust signals actually do something, because a generic seal is reported to do nothing to close a sale while specific, true statements can.

signal.check: The PDP or hero shows only generic security seals with no specific policy or proof statement near the CTA.

expected_effect.size: one case reports +18% revenue per session after 3 weeks from moving trust icons inline next to Add to Cart; no stats given

risk.note: Never invent a count or a press mention that is not true.

prerequisites: A real, substantiated credibility asset (reviews, guarantee, press, customer count)
steps: Remove generic footer security seals from hero and PDP unless a brand test says otherwise.
Add a specific, true policy or proof statement beside the CTA and in cart (returns, guarantee, customer count, press, made-in).
Keep payment logos in checkout, since those serve a different purpose.
Never invent a count or a press mention.

test.method: A/B test: specific proof statement versus generic seal or nothing.

title: Cut or restructure a long PDP text block that shows a steep scroll drop
hypothesis: If a PDP text block that shows a steep scroll drop right after it is turned into benefit-driven bullets with bold key words, then more shoppers reach add to cart, because the problem is usually presentation that blocks scanning, not the length itself.

signal.check: A scroll map shows a steep drop (well beyond normal end-of-page decay) right after a text block.

expected_effect.size: one example shows about a 30% drop right after a long paragraph, with only 25% reaching add to cart

risk.note: A copy restructure, easy to revert.

prerequisites: A scroll map showing the drop
steps: Find the exact section where the scroll drop is steep, not just normal decay.
Turn the block into benefit-driven bullets with bold key words, outcomes not features.
Keep detailed information for products that genuinely need it, but fix the presentation.

test.method: A/B test on the restructured copy block.
test.measure: Scroll reach past the block, cvr_pdp_to_cart

title: Answer the top 'almost did not buy' objection in the hero, and build the FAQ from real objections
hypothesis: If the top objection from the post-purchase survey is answered in the hero or beside the CTA, and the FAQ is built from real objections instead of shipping policy or brand story, then the page addresses what actually stops people from buying.

signal.check: The FAQ covers shipping policy and brand story with no top-objection theme from the post-purchase survey.

expected_effect.size: one case (leather-quality objection rewritten into the hero) reports $77,000 a month; another (results-timing objection) is described as illustrative

risk.note: A copy change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Post-purchase survey themes (CRO-031)
steps: Identify the top 'almost did not buy' theme from the post-purchase survey.
Rewrite the hero or a section beside the CTA to directly answer that objection.
Rebuild the FAQ from the top 3 real objections, not policy or brand story.
For any process that starts with a click (quiz, consultation), state exactly what happens after it.

test.method: A/B test on the hero or FAQ rewrite.

title: Send cold paid traffic to a message-matched landing page instead of a generic PDP
hypothesis: If cold, unaware traffic lands on a page matched to the ad's persona, offer and angle instead of a generic PDP listing every benefit, then more of that traffic converts, because a specific ad into a generic multi-benefit PDP undersells the one thing that made someone click.

signal.check: Active ad concepts with meaningful spend send traffic to a plain PDP or homepage with no matching landing page.

expected_effect.size: one pre-sell listicle case reports $20,000 a month and cold-traffic scaling; no baseline or sample given

risk.note: A new page build; the existing PDP stays untouched.

prerequisites: Active ad concepts by persona, offer and angle, with spend
steps: List active ad concepts with meaningful spend.
For each concept, check whether the landing destination matches its persona, offer and angle.
Build a message-matched page for concepts with real spend, keeping the page on one angle.
Match hero, mechanism, objections, testimonials and CTA to the ad's promise and wording.
Prioritise by spend, since each page adds build and QA cost.

test.method: A/B test: message-matched page versus the generic destination, for one ad concept.

title: Test pain-led or benefit-led headline framing against feature-led framing
hypothesis: If the PDP or landing-page headline is tested pain-led or benefit-led against the current feature-led version, then the store learns which framing actually converts, because headline framing is named as one of the few above-the-fold changes worth a split test at scale.

signal.check: The current headline is feature-led (specs, ingredients) with no pain-led or benefit-led version tested.

risk.note: A copy test, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Enough traffic to power the test per R53
steps: Write a pain-led or benefit-led headline as the challenger.
Keep everything else on the page constant.
Run as a big-swing A/B test, seen by everyone.

test.method: A/B test on headline framing.

title: Repeat one CTA as often as reach data justifies, and never stack competing offers
hypothesis: If a page repeats one clear action (hero, sticky bar, after proof, end) instead of offering several different actions, then shoppers are never asked to choose between competing offers, because friction rises whenever a page presents more than one destination.

signal.check: A page shows more than one distinct offer or destination competing for attention (buy now, subscribe, download a guide, book a call).

risk.note: A layout simplification.

steps: List every CTA on the page and the action or destination each points to.
Keep only one distinct action; repeat it at the hero, sticky bar, after proof and at the end.
Remove or demote any competing offer to a secondary page.
State what happens after the click for the one remaining CTA.

test.method: A/B test: single repeated CTA versus multiple competing CTAs.

title: Add a size guide or fit tool next to the size picker on apparel and footwear PDPs
hypothesis: If a size chart, fit quiz or measurements-to-size table sits next to the size picker, then fewer shoppers abandon from fit uncertainty or buy the wrong size and return it, because a shopper who cannot judge fit either leaves or guesses wrong.

signal.check: The store's size-related return rate is high and no size guide or fit tool sits near the size picker.

does_not_apply_when: Products with no size dependency

risk.note: A PDP addition, easy to remove.

prerequisites: Size-related return rate by SKU
steps: Pull the size-related return rate for apparel, footwear or other size-dependent SKUs.
Build or install a size chart, fit quiz or measurements-to-size table.
Place it directly next to the size picker.
Track add-to-cart and size-related returns after launch.

test.method: A/B test or before-and-after on size-related return rate.
test.read_point: After enough orders to compare return rates

title: Show a buy-now-pay-later badge on the PDP and cart for mid to high-AOV items
hypothesis: If a mid to high-AOV item shows an instalment badge (Afterpay-style) on the PDP and in cart, then a considered purchase feels more affordable today, because splitting the price into instalments lowers the perceived commitment.

signal.check: A mid to high-AOV product shows no instalment or buy-now-pay-later option on the PDP or in cart.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named with no card id and no built rule

does_not_apply_when: Low-price impulse items
luxury positioning where instalments can cheapen the brand

risk.note: Verify the instalment provider's fees and brand fit before enabling broadly.

prerequisites: An instalment payment provider integrated
steps: Confirm the store carries mid to high-AOV items suited to instalments.
Integrate an instalment provider if not already live.
Add the instalment badge to the PDP near price, and in cart.
Verify against brand data before treating this as proven; no source builds a rule on it.

test.method: A/B test: badge present versus absent, on mid to high-AOV PDPs.

title: Move a high-click, low-reach homepage module higher on the page
hypothesis: If a homepage module with a high share of clicks but low scroll reach is moved higher, with the same design and destination, then more of the demand already shown by its click share gets captured, because the module's current position is hiding it from most visitors.

signal.check: An Area map shows a homepage module with a high click share reached by only a minority of visitors.

expected_effect.size: one case reports a module with 10.41% of homepage clicks reached by only 30 to 35% of visitors, and an 18% conversion lift after moving it, with no statistics given

risk.note: A layout move, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Area map and scroll map for the homepage
steps: Identify the module with high click share and low scroll reach from the Area map.
Move it higher on the page, keeping the same design and destination.
Confirm intent versus confusion in recordings before finalising the hypothesis.

test.method: A/B test: module moved up versus current position.

title: Restyle or remove homepage modules that are highly visible but get almost no clicks
hypothesis: If a highly visible homepage module getting very few clicks is restyled or removed, then screen space goes to something that actually earns clicks, because weak relevance, unclear affordance or a low-priority need is likely wasting that space.

signal.check: A homepage module sits in a high-reach position but gets a very small share of clicks in the Area map.

risk.note: A layout change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Area map for the homepage
steps: Identify highly visible modules with very low click share.
Watch recordings to check whether it is confusion, low relevance or unclear affordance.
Restyle to make the module's action clearer, or remove it and reclaim the space.

test.method: A/B test: restyled or removed module versus current.

title: Address alternatives and cheaper options at the end of PDP copy instead of staying silent
hypothesis: If the PDP copy addresses existing alternatives and cheaper options near the end, then shoppers who are comparing do not leave to search for a comparison the page could have made for them, because staying silent on alternatives leaves the comparison to a competitor's page.

signal.check: The PDP copy never mentions how the product compares to cheaper or existing alternatives.

risk.note: A copy addition.

prerequisites: Knowledge of the store's real alternatives and how the product compares
steps: List the realistic alternatives a shopper might be comparing.
Write a short, honest section addressing why this product versus those alternatives.
Place it near the end of the PDP copy.

test.method: A/B test on the added section.

title: Tailor PDP facts for AI-referred visitors so they do not have to re-browse
hypothesis: If the PDP confirms product type, size, price, delivery and use case immediately for AI-referred visitors, then those visitors convert instead of leaving to re-browse, because AI-referred traffic already arrives pre-sold on a specific answer and a generic page forces them to start over.

signal.check: AI referral traffic is not segmented, or a segmented check shows a generic PDP with no quick facts summary.

risk.note: A PDP content addition.

prerequisites: Ability to segment AI referral traffic in GA4
steps: Segment AI referral traffic and read its landing mix and conversion rate.
Add a quick facts summary confirming product type, size, price, delivery and use case at the top of the PDP.
Measure revenue per session for this segment before and after.

test.method: Before-and-after or A/B test on the quick facts summary, segmented to AI-referred traffic.
test.read_point: At planned sample or after enough AI-referred sessions

title: Remove the cart discount-code box whenever no promotion is live
hypothesis: If the discount-code box is hidden from cart whenever no promotion is live, then fewer shoppers leave to search for a code, hit a coupon site, and never return, because a visible empty coupon field invites exactly that detour.

signal.check: The cart shows a discount-code box even when no promotion is currently running.

expected_effect.size: part of a combined $40,000-a-month cart result; no isolated figure

risk.note: A conditional display change.

prerequisites: Ability to conditionally show or hide the coupon field
steps: Check whether a promotion is currently live.
Hide the discount-code box in cart when no promotion is live.
Keep it working and visible when one is.

test.method: A/B test or ship as a repair.
test.read_point: At planned sample, or a few weeks after shipping

title: Add a returns, support and guarantee reassurance bar in the cart
hypothesis: If the cart shows a reassurance bar (returns, support, satisfaction or money-back guarantee) near the checkout button, then a hesitant shopper gets a final nudge of trust right before committing, because reassurance placed at the point of highest doubt is most effective.

signal.check: The cart page has no returns, support or guarantee reassurance near the checkout button.

risk.note: A cart addition, easy to revert.

prerequisites: A true returns and guarantee policy to state
steps: Confirm the store's returns and guarantee policy.
Add a reassurance bar (easy returns, support, satisfaction guarantee) near the checkout button.
Keep the statement specific and true, not a generic seal.

test.method: A/B test on the reassurance bar.

title: Use the cart drawer to raise RPV with a free-shipping threshold, bundle upgrade or in-cart upsell
hypothesis: If the cart drawer shows a free-shipping progress message set above the typical cart value, a bundle upgrade, or a relevant in-cart upsell, then RPV rises instead of just AOV, because these levers can raise both order value and completion when priced against real margin.

signal.check: The cart drawer shows no free-shipping progress message, no upgrade path and no upsell.

expected_effect.size: one case reports nearly $60,000 a month with AOV lifted from a prior $60 to $80 range using in-cart upsells

risk.note: Check margin and fulfilment cost before setting the threshold or bundle discount.

prerequisites: Typical cart value
fulfilment cost per order
steps: Pull typical cart value and fulfilment cost per order.
Set the free-shipping threshold above the typical cart value.
Add a 1-click upgrade from a single item to a bundle or routine.
Add relevant, low-friction in-cart upsells.
Judge the result on RPV and contribution, not AOV alone.

test.method: A/B test on the cart drawer additions.

title: Test a multi-buy offer below add to cart for low-price consumables people own several of
hypothesis: If a low-price consumable category tests a multi-buy offer (buy 3, save 20%) below add to cart, then AOV and units per order rise, because this fits products people naturally own several of, not a considered or luxury purchase.

signal.check: The store sells low-price consumables people own multiples of, with no multi-buy offer tested below add to cart.

expected_effect.size: one case (sunglasses, $30 to $40 products) reports over $180,000 a month; no baseline given

does_not_apply_when: Luxury or considered-purchase categories

risk.note: Check margin on the multi-buy discount before launch.

prerequisites: Gross margin at the proposed discount level
steps: Confirm the category is low-price and consumable, with plausible multi-unit ownership.
Check margin holds at the proposed multi-buy discount.
Add the multi-buy offer below the add-to-cart button.
Judge the result on RPV and contribution.

test.method: A/B test on the multi-buy offer.

title: Cap total checkout extras under about 10% of AOV and show them before checkout begins
hypothesis: If shipping, tax and fees are summed and kept under about 10% of AOV, shown before checkout begins with no drip pricing, then checkout abandonment from surprise costs drops, because late extra costs are the most cited reason for abandonment.

signal.check: Checkout extras (shipping, tax, fees) exceed about 10% of AOV, or are only revealed at the last step.

expected_effect.size: 39% of abandoners cite late extra costs as cited from Baymard (verify current figures)

risk.note: Ship as a repair; most checkout changes cannot be A/B tested on standard Shopify.

prerequisites: Checkout extra costs as % of AOV, current Baymard figures for reference
steps: Sum shipping, tax and fees on a typical order.
Check the total against about 10% of AOV.
Show the total cost before checkout begins; remove any drip pricing.
If tax is included but shown as a line, label it clearly.

test.method: Ship as a repair; measure with before-and-after stage rates as weak evidence.
test.read_point: A few weeks after the change

title: Make guest checkout the default and prominent option, collecting email during it
hypothesis: If guest checkout is the clear default with email collected during it, and account creation is offered after purchase, then fewer shoppers abandon at a forced account step, because a large share of sites reportedly do not make guest checkout prominent enough.

signal.check: Checkout forces or strongly nudges account creation before guest checkout is available.

expected_effect.size: 62% of sites do not make guest checkout prominent enough, as cited from Baymard (verify current figures)

risk.note: A settings change.

prerequisites: Shopify customer-account setting access
steps: Check the current customer-account setting for forced or optional accounts.
Make guest checkout the default and visually prominent.
Collect email as part of the guest flow.
Offer account creation after purchase completes.

test.method: Ship as a repair.
test.read_point: A few weeks after the change

title: Put express payment methods first in checkout, including local methods for the market
hypothesis: If Shop Pay, Apple Pay and Google Pay (or UPI in India) are placed at the top of checkout with recognisable payment brands and no redirects, then fewer shoppers abandon over payment friction, because express methods remove the manual entry step entirely.

signal.check: Express payment methods are missing, buried, or the checkout redirects or context-switches during payment.

risk.note: A settings and placement change.

prerequisites: Wallet integrations enabled for the store's markets
steps: Confirm Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay (and UPI in India) are enabled.
Move them to the top of the checkout page.
Remove any redirect or context switch during payment where possible.

test.method: Ship as a repair.
test.read_point: A few weeks after the change

title: Cut checkout fields to the strictly necessary and enable autofill
hypothesis: If checkout fields are cut to only what is truly needed and autofill is enabled, then fewer shoppers abandon mid-checkout, because a typical site's checkout reportedly averages over 11 fields and every extra field is a chance to leave.

signal.check: Checkout has more fields than are used, no autofill, or no progress indicator on a multi-step flow.

expected_effect.size: Baymard average is 11.3 checkout fields (verify current figures)

risk.note: Only remove fields the store does not actually use downstream.

prerequisites: List of fields actually used by fulfilment, marketing and support
steps: Count and list every checkout field currently shown.
Remove or make optional any field the store does not actually use.
Shorten the address block where possible.
Enable autofill.
Add a progress indicator on any multi-step flow.

test.method: Ship as a repair.
test.read_point: A few weeks after the change

title: State the returns policy plainly at the decision point without rushing to free returns
hypothesis: If the returns policy is stated plainly at the point of decision, and free returns are only adopted where profitable, then shoppers get the reassurance they need without the store absorbing a cost it cannot afford, because rushing into free returns, above all in fashion, can be a margin decision made on opinion.

signal.check: The returns policy is hidden or hard to find during checkout, or free returns were adopted without a profitability check.

risk.note: Test and accept some return-rate cost only if it is more profitable overall.

prerequisites: Current return rate and cost of returns
steps: Surface the returns policy plainly during checkout, not hidden in a footer link.
Check the profitability of free returns against current return-rate cost, above all in fashion.
Test any policy change before rolling it out broadly.

test.method: A/B test on returns policy visibility or terms.

title: Test one-page versus multi-step checkout instead of assuming which converts better
hypothesis: If checkout structure (one-page versus multi-step) is decided by a test instead of opinion, then the store avoids changing a working checkout on a guess, because one marketplace test found the opposite of the usual advice, with the 3-page checkout raising AOV and RPV.

signal.check: Checkout structure was last changed based on opinion, with no test behind the decision.

expected_effect.size: one marketplace switchback (12 days, hourly rotation) found the 3-page checkout raised AOV 2.1% at 98% significance

does_not_apply_when: Standard Shopify plan without Plus or server-side testing capability

risk.note: Requires Shopify Plus or server-side testing since standard checkout cannot be A/B tested client-side.

prerequisites: Shopify Plus checkout extensibility, or server-side testing capability
steps: Confirm the store has Shopify Plus checkout extensibility or a server-side testing setup.
Build both a one-page and a multi-step checkout variant.
Set RPV as the primary metric where it can be powered.
Run the test and read the result rather than deciding on opinion.

test.method: A/B test on checkout structure, on Plus or server-side.

title: Get faster delivery options before considering hiding delivery dates
hypothesis: If faster delivery options are pursued before any test of hiding delivery dates, then the store fixes the real problem instead of masking it, because hiding dates adds ambiguity and is reported to lower conversion on its own.

signal.check: Delivery is slow and the team is considering hiding delivery-time estimates instead of speeding up fulfilment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; hiding dates is reported to lower conversion, so the fix is faster delivery, not concealment

does_not_apply_when: No legal review of delivery disclosure rules has been done

risk.note: Only test hiding dates with legal review and a properly sized runtime.

prerequisites: Current fulfilment days
legal review of delivery disclosure rules if hiding is considered
steps: Check current delivery speed and where it lags competitors.
Work with sourcing or fulfilment to offer faster shipping options first.
Only consider testing hidden delivery dates with a legal review and a properly sized test, never as a first move.

test.method: Before-and-after or A/B test on delivery speed options; a hidden-date test only with legal review.

title: Ship checkout changes as repairs on standard Shopify plans, since client-side testing is not possible
hypothesis: If checkout hypotheses on standard Shopify plans are shipped as repairs instead of planned as client-side tests, then the team never wastes effort designing a test the platform cannot run, because checkout extensibility replaced checkout.liquid and there is no built-in way to show a checkout change to only one group on standard plans.

signal.check: A checkout A/B test is planned on a standard (non-Plus) Shopify plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning correction, not a lift on its own

does_not_apply_when: Store is on Shopify Plus with checkout extensibility

risk.note: A planning correction.

prerequisites: Shopify plan tier confirmed
steps: Check the store's Shopify plan tier and checkout extensibility status.
On standard plans, plan every checkout hypothesis as a repair, not a client-side test.
Test everything before checkout (product, collection, cart, homepage) as normal.
For theme-level tests, consider Shopify Rollouts and compute the statistics manually since it gives no significance verdict.
Re-verify plan and platform limits yearly.

test.method: Repair with before-and-after monitoring for checkout; standard A/B for everything before checkout.
test.read_point: A few weeks after any checkout repair

title: Localise checkout currency, cash-on-delivery and tax display for each market the store sells into
hypothesis: If checkout shows the shopper's own currency, offers cash on delivery where it is the norm, and shows GST-inclusive pricing as one number, then a shopper never abandons over a payment method or price display that feels wrong for their market.

signal.check: The store sells into more than one country or language and checkout does not localise currency, payment method or tax display.

does_not_apply_when: Single-market store with no cross-border or multi-currency traffic

risk.note: A localisation build.

prerequisites: Local payment norms and tax display rules by market
steps: Check local payment norms, cash-on-delivery expectations and tax display rules for each market.
Ensure currency does not switch mid-checkout.
Add cash on delivery where it is the market norm.
Show GST-inclusive or tax-inclusive pricing as one number, not a surprise line.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test where traffic allows per market.
test.read_point: A few weeks after the change

title: Put about 90% of CRO effort on mobile and audit every page on a phone
hypothesis: If most CRO effort and every audit happen on a phone first, then the store optimises for where most traffic and sales actually happen, because mobile can carry 60 to 95% of traffic depending on the brand and converts at roughly half the desktop rate.

signal.check: Recent CRO work (audits, redesigns, tests) was done desktop-first with no mobile check.

expected_effect.size: mobile is reported at 60 to 95% of traffic depending on brand; mobile converts at about half the desktop rate

does_not_apply_when: A genuinely desktop-researched, high-ticket purchase category

risk.note: A prioritisation shift.

prerequisites: Device split known
steps: Check the device split for traffic and sales.
Re-order the audit and test backlog to put mobile work first.
Check every page on a phone, not a desktop preview, before shipping anything.
Set tap targets to at least 44px, put key actions in the thumb zone, and use wallets and guest checkout by default.

test.method: Not a test; a prioritisation shift applied to the whole programme.
test.measure: Share of backlog items that are mobile-first

title: Treat mobile page speed as a CRO lever and isolate its revenue effect with a test or holdout
hypothesis: If mobile speed is measured with real-user data and its revenue effect is isolated with a test or holdout, then speed work gets credited (or not) accurately, because the commonly cited speed elasticities contradict each other and should prompt investigation, not a forecast.

signal.check: Mobile LCP is at or above 2.5 seconds with no test or holdout isolating its revenue impact.

expected_effect.size: cited elasticities disagree (100ms = 3.5% lower conversion; 100ms = 7% drop; 1s = up to 7%); treat as directional only

risk.note: Speed work itself lives in 08-SPD; this idea is about measuring its CRO impact.

prerequisites: Real-user LCP data on mobile
a speed improvement already planned or shipped via 08-SPD
steps: Pull real-user mobile LCP for the store's key pages.
Target under 2 seconds for mobile LCP, hero images under 100KB, grid images under 60KB.
Coordinate the actual speed fix with 08-SPD.
Isolate the revenue effect of the speed change with an A/B test or holdout rather than assuming a fixed elasticity.

test.method: A/B test or holdout isolating the speed change's revenue effect.

title: Give every email or SMS capture CTA a lure that matches the shopper's stage
hypothesis: If a capture CTA offers a lure matched to the shopper's stage (a buyer guide for someone unsure what to buy, a discount or free postage for someone who knows but delays), then more of the right visitors opt in for the right reason, because a bare 'subscribe to our newsletter' offers nothing to act on.

signal.check: A capture CTA says only 'subscribe' or 'join our list' with no specific lure.

risk.note: Check discount and shipping cost against margin before offering them as a lure.

prerequisites: Margin data to check discount and shipping cost against
steps: Identify the shopper's likely stage at each capture point.
Offer a buyer guide for shoppers who do not know what to buy.
Offer a first-order discount or free postage for shoppers who know but delay.
Check the discount and shipping cost against margin first.
Measure signup-to-first-purchase rate, not just signup volume.

test.method: A/B test on the capture CTA lure.

title: Ask about the shopper's need before asking for contact details in a quiz or multi-step flow
hypothesis: If a quiz asks about the shopper's problem or need before asking for name, email or phone, then it feels like a diagnosis instead of a lead-capture form, because asking contact details first signals the opposite of what the shopper expected.

signal.check: A quiz or multi-step flow asks for contact details before asking about the shopper's need.

risk.note: A flow-order change.

prerequisites: An existing quiz or multi-step flow
steps: Reorder the quiz so need-based questions come first.
Move contact-detail collection to after the diagnostic questions.
Be honest with the shopper about what the result step actually delivers.

test.method: A/B test on the reordered flow.

title: State what happens after the click and lower commitment language on any CTA that starts a process
hypothesis: If any CTA that starts a process (quiz, consultation, pre-order, subscription) says what happens next and uses permission language like 'no obligation', then fewer people hesitate to click, because people assume the worst about an unexplained next step.

signal.check: A CTA that starts a multi-step process does not say what happens after the click.

expected_effect.size: one lead-gen case reports a 60% difference between 'get a free quote' and 'book a free survey'; no sample given, and lead-gen origin

risk.note: A copy change.

steps: List every CTA that starts a multi-step process.
Add a short line stating what happens after the click.
Use permission phrases such as 'no obligation' where true.

test.method: A/B test on the CTA copy.
test.measure: Click-through and completion rate on the process

title: Audit on-site search as its own funnel with autocomplete and no-results handling
hypothesis: If on-site search is audited for autocomplete quality, no-results handling and search-to-purchase rate, then a shopper who already told the store what they want stops hitting a dead end, because a slow or irrelevant search wastes the clearest intent signal on the site.

signal.check: Search carries a material share of sessions and has never been checked for search-to-purchase rate or zero-result queries.

does_not_apply_when: Search carries a negligible share of sessions

risk.note: An audit and fix, low risk.

prerequisites: Search usage share and top zero-result queries
steps: Check search usage share and top zero-result queries.
Track search-to-purchase rate next to browse-to-purchase rate.
Fix or improve autocomplete relevance.
Fix the no-results page to route to relevant categories instead of a dead end.
Treat a big gap between search and browse purchase rates as a hypothesis source.

test.method: Before-and-after or A/B test on search improvements.
test.read_point: At planned sample or a few weeks after the fix

title: Build a distinct hypothesis set for subscription pause, skip, swap and cancel-flow saves
hypothesis: If subscription mechanics (pause, skip, swap, cancel-flow saves) get their own hypothesis set separate from one-off purchase CRO, then subscribers who want to pause or skip find how, and a cancel flow can offer a pause, swap or discount before the cancel confirms, because a subscriber who cannot find pause or skip will cancel instead.

signal.check: The store has subscription SKUs or plans but no dedicated pause, skip, swap or cancel-save flow.

does_not_apply_when: Pure one-off catalogue with no subscription offering

risk.note: A flow build, testable independently of one-off CRO work.

prerequisites: Subscription platform with pause, skip and cancel-flow customisation
steps: Check whether pause, skip and swap options are easy to find in the subscriber account.
Build a cancel flow that offers a pause, a swap or a discount before the cancel confirms.
Track save rate at each offered step.
Keep this hypothesis set separate from one-off purchase CRO work.

test.method: A/B test on the cancel-flow save offers.
test.read_point: At planned sample of cancel attempts

title: Keep attribution questions like 'how did you hear about us' out of CRO research surveys
hypothesis: If attribution questions are kept in a separate survey from CRO objection research, then post-purchase survey answers stay focused on purchase objections and motivations, because mixing the two survey types confuses two different jobs: measurement and hypothesis generation.

signal.check: A post-purchase or exit survey mixes 'how did you hear about us' with objection or motivation questions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this improves research quality rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A survey design fix.

prerequisites: Existing post-purchase or exit survey
steps: Review the current survey questions for attribution content mixed with CRO questions.
Move attribution questions to a separate 06-MEA survey.
Keep the CRO survey focused on purchase objections and motivations.

test.method: Not a test; a survey design fix.

title: Never show different prices for the same SKU to different shoppers at the same time
hypothesis: If price tests never show the same SKU at different prices to different shoppers at the same time, then the store avoids legal disclosure issues and a brand-trust landmine, because even where personalised pricing is legal, discovery of it has historically caused a serious backlash.

signal.check: A proposed test would show two prices for the same SKU to different users at the same time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this avoids a legal and trust risk rather than lifting a metric

risk.note: A discovered same-SKU price test can trigger refund demands and lasting brand damage; treat as a hard rule, not a test to run.

prerequisites: Jurisdiction rules on personalised pricing and disclosure
steps: Rule out any test that shows two prices for the same SKU to different users at once.
Test price presentation, savings framing, payment framing, tiers, bundles or different offerings instead.
Check jurisdiction rules on personalised pricing and disclosure before any offer-based price test.
Document refund, support and price-match handling before exposing traffic to any offer test.

test.method: Not a test to run; a hard constraint on all price and offer tests.
test.read_point: Before any price or offer test is designed

title: Run offer tests on a monthly cadence when the store cannot power micro-tests
hypothesis: If a store under about 300,000 monthly sessions runs one offer test a month (buy-1-get-1, 3-for-2, build-a-bundle, thresholds, gifts with purchase, post-purchase upsell) instead of many small tweaks, then it learns steadily without wasting effort on underpowered tests.

signal.check: The store is under about 300,000 monthly sessions and has not run an offer test in the current month.

expected_effect.size: one gift-with-purchase example uses about $30 perceived value against $4 to $5 COGS for orders over $60; one post-purchase upsell example is $19 (usually $35 to $40) at 50% off for 5 minutes

risk.note: Check margin before committing to any offer.

prerequisites: Margin data for the proposed offer
steps: Pick one offer type for the month: multi-buy, bundle, threshold, gift-with-purchase, or post-purchase upsell.
Check the offer's cost against perceived value and margin.
Launch and judge on RPV and contribution, not AOV alone.

test.method: A/B test or before-and-after on the offer, per traffic band.
test.read_point: At planned sample, or end of month

title: Prefer a positioned offer over a blanket discount
hypothesis: If a positioned offer (a themed bundle at full price, a free-shipping threshold set to pull AOV up) replaces a blanket discount, then revenue and margin both hold up better, because a blanket discount can lift revenue while cutting profit and training customers to wait for the next sale.

signal.check: The store runs frequent sitewide discounts, or offers free shipping with no threshold or too low a threshold.

expected_effect.size: one case (a themed bundle at full price) reportedly converted better than the product ever did on sale; no baseline given

risk.note: A merchandising change.

prerequisites: Current discount rate and free-shipping threshold
steps: Replace a blanket discount with a themed bundle or positioned offer at full price.
Set the free-shipping threshold high enough to pull AOV up, not just to hand out free shipping.
Track discount rate and gross margin before and after.

test.method: A/B test or before-and-after on the offer type.
test.read_point: At planned sample or after a full promo cycle

title: Match the test method to the platform: client-side for visuals, server-side for checkout and pricing logic
hypothesis: If client-side tools are reserved for front-end visuals and server-side or Shopify Rollouts are used for checkout, pricing logic and speed-sensitive paths, then each test uses the method that fits its risk profile, because client-side tools flicker and expose logic publicly, while server-side avoids that at the cost of an engineer and a deploy cycle.

signal.check: A checkout, pricing-logic or speed-sensitive test is planned with a client-side visual editor tool.

risk.note: A tooling decision.

prerequisites: Testing tool inventory and Shopify plan tier
steps: Classify the planned test as a visual change or a checkout, pricing-logic or speed-sensitive change.
Use a client-side visual editor for the former.
Use server-side testing or Shopify Rollouts for the latter.
Record the platform constraint in the test brief.

test.method: Not a test; a tooling decision applied before every test plan.

title: Check the Shopify plan tier and re-verify it yearly before planning any test
hypothesis: If the Shopify plan tier and its testing options are checked before every engagement and re-verified yearly, then the test plan never assumes a capability the store's plan does not have, because Basic, Shopify and Advanced plans differ from Plus in what can be tested and how.

signal.check: The store's Shopify plan tier has not been confirmed in the last year, or a test plan assumes checkout extensibility on a non-Plus plan.

risk.note: A verification step.

steps: Confirm the current Shopify plan tier.
On Basic, Shopify or Advanced, plan tests only before checkout (product, collection, cart, homepage, add to cart, trust elements, pricing display).
On Plus, checkout extensibility and native theme A/B become available.
Re-verify plan tier and checkout options yearly, since Shopify's offerings change.

test.method: Not a test; a verification step at the start of every engagement.

title: Confirm the testing vendor's stats engine, prior, SRM alerting and free tier before committing
hypothesis: If a testing vendor's stats engine, prior (if Bayesian), SRM alerting and free tier are confirmed before committing, then the store does not discover a stats-engine surprise mid-programme, because vendors differ meaningfully on these points and change them over time.

signal.check: A testing tool was chosen with no check of its current stats engine, prior, SRM alerting or free tier.

risk.note: A vendor-verification step.

prerequisites: Vendor documentation for the candidate tool
steps: Check the vendor's current stats engine (frequentist, Bayesian, sequential) in its own docs.
Confirm the prior used if Bayesian.
Confirm the SRM alerting threshold.
Confirm the current free tier limits before budgeting.

test.method: Not a test; a vendor-verification step before tool commitment.
test.read_point: Before choosing or renewing a testing tool

title: Run a comprehensive testing programme only above the traffic and order gates, big swings below
hypothesis: If a comprehensive programme (deep audits, 4 to 8 isolated tests a month, a full data stack) only runs above about 300,000 monthly sessions with adequate orders, and every store below that runs big swings instead, then the programme's ambition always matches what the traffic can actually support.

signal.check: A store under the traffic gate is running a comprehensive testing programme with weekly test launches.

risk.note: A programme-scope decision.

prerequisites: Monthly sessions and order count
steps: Check monthly sessions and order count against the comprehensive-programme gate (about 300,000 sessions with adequate orders).
Above the gate, run deep audits, isolated A/B tests at 4 to 8 a month, and a learning loop on wins and losses.
Below it, run the big-swing approach from R54 instead.

test.method: Not a test; a programme-scope decision.
test.read_point: At programme planning, and whenever traffic crosses the gate

title: Cap monthly PDP, cart and checkout tests to what the store's traffic can power, with no page-area overlap
hypothesis: If the number of PDP, cart and checkout tests run each month is capped to what the store's weekly order volume can power, with no two tests overlapping one page area, then the programme never runs an underpowered test just to hit a cadence target, because cadence should be an output of power, not an input.

signal.check: A weekly testing cadence is set as a target regardless of the store's order volume.

risk.note: A planning cap.

prerequisites: Weekly order volume
test calendar (see CRO-058)
steps: Compute how many tests the store's weekly order volume can power at the chosen MDE.
Set that number as the monthly cap, not a fixed cadence target.
Never run 2 tests on the same page area at once.
Below 300 orders a month, run 1 bold test at a time, not a weekly cadence.

test.method: Not a test; a cadence cap applied to the whole programme.

title: Check the evidence gate before blaming a low programme win rate on the ideas themselves
hypothesis: If a low win rate triggers a check of whether the evidence gate (2+ points of evidence per idea) is actually being enforced, then the team fixes the real cause of a weak win rate, because research-prequalified programmes report meaningfully higher win rates than unresearched ones.

signal.check: A programme's win rate is low and no one has checked whether the evidence gate is actually enforced.

expected_effect.size: one source cites a 36.3% win rate tied to a programme with research pre-qualification

risk.note: A diagnostic check, not a change on its own.

prerequisites: Historical win rate
backlog evidence records
steps: Compute the current win rate and its definition.
If it is below the 10 to 20% anchor, check whether backlog entries actually have 2+ points of evidence.
Tighten enforcement of the evidence gate if it has slipped.

test.method: Not a test; a diagnostic check on the programme.
test.measure: Win rate before and after tightening the evidence gate

title: Test loyalty and rewards programme changes on repeat rate, separate from first-purchase CRO
hypothesis: If loyalty or rewards programme changes (sign-up placement, point-earning clarity, redemption friction) are tested on repeat rate and RPV instead of folded into first-purchase CRO, then the store measures the right outcome for a programme that only affects repeat buyers.

signal.check: The store has a loyalty or rewards programme, or is considering one, with no dedicated repeat-rate testing track.

does_not_apply_when: Store has no loyalty or rewards programme and is not considering one

risk.note: A programme-mechanics test, separate from first-purchase CRO.

prerequisites: A loyalty or rewards programme, existing or planned
steps: List loyalty programme touchpoints: sign-up placement, point-earning clarity, redemption friction.
Set up a separate hypothesis track for these, measured on repeat rate and RPV.
Keep this track distinct from first-purchase conversion tests.

test.method: A/B test on a loyalty programme touchpoint.
test.read_point: At planned sample, tracked over repeat purchase cycles

title: Repair popups, chat widgets and cookie bars that cover add to cart or the cart button
hypothesis: If a popup firing in the first 5 seconds, a chat widget sitting over add to cart, or a cookie bar covering the cart button is repaired immediately instead of tested, then no shopper is deliberately left on a known blocker, because these show up consistently as rage clicks and in self-purchase audits.

signal.check: Self-purchase audits, rage-click data or recordings show a popup, chat widget or cookie bar covering a key purchase-path button.

risk.note: A repair, not a test; fixing an overlay blocking a purchase button has little downside.

prerequisites: Recordings or self-purchase audit findings
steps: Check recordings and rage-click data for popups, chat widgets or cookie bars over add to cart or the cart button.
Confirm the finding in a self-purchase audit on mobile and desktop.
Delay, move or resize the overlay so it never covers a purchase-path button.
Log it as a repair, not a test, and verify with fresh recordings.

test.method: Not a test; repair and verify with fresh recordings.
test.measure: Rage-click rate on the affected button, fresh recordings

title: Run the CLOSER six-part audit before writing a page hypothesis
hypothesis: If any page that asks a shopper to act is scored on credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use and result, then missing persuasion elements surface before a hypothesis is written, because a page can look fine and still be missing one of these six things.

signal.check: No page in the backlog has been scored against the six CLOSER elements before a hypothesis was written for it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a qualitative audit, not a lift estimate

risk.note: An audit method, not a site change.

prerequisites: Access to the page being audited
steps: Pick the exact page a visitor lands on, not the homepage by default.
Score credibility: is there a clear reason to believe the business is good at this?
Score lure: does the CTA offer something the visitor actually wants?
Score objection handling: are fears about acting removed?
Score social proof, ease of use and result the same way.
Mark each element present, weak or missing, then rank gaps by likely effect and cost.

test.method: Not a test on its own; feed the gaps into the normal hypothesis and prioritisation process.
test.measure: Number of CLOSER elements present per audited page
test.read_point: Before any hypothesis for that page enters the backlog

title: Write proof copy with specific, named detail instead of vague praise
hypothesis: If testimonials and proof copy carry specific, checkable detail such as an age, a number or a named use case, then shoppers find the proof more believable, because vague praise gives no reason to trust it while a concrete detail builds belief even when it did not cause the result.

signal.check: Testimonials and proof statements on the PDP use generic praise (great product, love it) with no specific, checkable detail.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source claims specifics build belief, not a measured lift

risk.note: A copy edit, easy to revert.

prerequisites: A pool of real reviews or testimonials to mine for specific detail
steps: Pull real reviews or testimonials and find any specific, checkable detail: a number, an age, a named use case.
Rewrite featured proof to lead with that detail instead of general praise.
Show a few different kinds of customers, not one repeated profile.
Only use details that are true and permissioned.

test.method: Ship as a copy repair, or A/B test if the page has enough traffic.

title: Build credibility with niche language or founder story before reviews exist
hypothesis: If a new store with few or no reviews builds credibility through narrow, customer-specific language or a founder story instead of waiting for review volume, then shoppers get a reason to trust the page sooner, because a very specific description of the customer's exact problem can stand in for review proof.
does_not_apply_when: Store already has a working review volume

signal.check: The store has fewer than about 20 reviews and PDP copy reads as generic rather than speaking to one specific customer situation.

risk.note: A copy change with no reviews at stake.

prerequisites: A clear picture of the store's narrowest, most specific customer
steps: Write the product description to nail one narrow customer's exact situation, not a broad audience.
Add the founder's own relevant story where it is true and relevant.
Use a trusted endorser the audience already knows, if one exists.
Replace this with review-based proof once review volume builds.

test.method: Ship as a copy repair; not a test at zero review volume.

title: Build a credibility asset inventory mapped to specific shopper doubts
hypothesis: If every credibility asset (reviews, certifications, press mentions, warranty terms, years trading, customer counts) is listed and matched to the specific doubt it answers, then proof gets placed where it answers a real question instead of sitting on one hub page, because a doubt with no matching asset next to it stays unanswered.

signal.check: No inventory exists of the store's credibility assets and which shopper doubt each one answers.

risk.note: A cataloguing exercise before any page change.

prerequisites: List of top shopper doubts from surveys, reviews or support tickets
steps: List every credibility asset the store has: reviews, certifications, ingredient or material facts, press mentions, warranty terms, customer counts, years trading.
List the top shopper doubts from surveys, reviews and support tickets.
Match each asset to the doubt it answers.
Place each asset next to the moment that doubt comes up, not only on an About or proof page.
Update the inventory as new proof arrives.

test.method: Not a test; a mapping exercise that feeds page placement changes.
test.measure: Share of top doubts with a matching asset placed at the decision point
test.read_point: After the inventory is built and placed

title: Show product-matched proof on collection and bundle pages, not only the PDP
hypothesis: If collection and bundle pages carry reviews or proof matched to the specific products shown, not just the PDP, then shoppers get a reason to trust items before they click through, because proof placed only on individual PDPs misses shoppers who decide while still browsing.

signal.check: Collection and bundle pages show products with no matched rating, review count or proof, while PDPs carry this proof.

risk.note: An additive display change on existing pages.

prerequisites: Review data available per SKU or product
steps: Check whether collection and bundle pages show a rating or review count per product.
Add SKU-matched rating and review count to collection grid cards.
Add matched proof, such as a rating or a key review quote, to bundle pages for each included product.
Avoid showing generic, unmatched proof; keep it specific to the product shown.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test if collection traffic is high enough.
