test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and click-through from collection to PDP

title: Keep primary navigation and CTA patterns conventional, not novel
hypothesis: If primary navigation and the main call-to-action use familiar, recognisable patterns instead of novel or clever UI, then more shoppers find and use them, because an unfamiliar menu icon or interaction can hide the exact controls a distracted, unfamiliar visitor needs.
does_not_apply_when: Non-critical design areas away from navigation and the main CTA, where novelty is lower risk

signal.check: The main navigation or CTA uses a non-standard icon, label or interaction that user tests or recordings show visitors missing or hesitating over.

risk.note: Reverting to a standard pattern is low risk.

prerequisites: Recordings or a user test showing hesitation on the current pattern
steps: Watch recordings or run a small user test on the current navigation and main CTA.
Flag any novel icon, label or interaction that causes hesitation or a miss.
Replace it with the familiar, expected pattern, such as a standard menu icon or a clearly labelled button.
Reserve novelty for non-critical design areas away from navigation and the main CTA.

test.method: Ship as a repair; test only if the change is large enough to size properly.
test.measure: cvr_overall, or task success rate in a user test
test.read_point: After the change, or after the next user-test round

title: Use dynamic call tracking for phone-assisted ecommerce purchases
hypothesis: If a store that takes orders by phone uses dynamic number insertion instead of one static number, then each call can be attributed to its traffic source and keyword, because a single phone number gives no channel or campaign data on its own.
does_not_apply_when: Store takes no phone orders and has no phone-assisted buying path

signal.check: The store lists one static phone number as a buying channel, with no way to see which channel or keyword drove the call.

risk.note: A tracking change, not a purchase-path change.

prerequisites: A phone-order buying path already in use
Ad platform and analytics accounts to connect call data to
steps: Confirm the store has a real phone-assisted buying path worth attributing.
Set up dynamic number insertion so each visitor session sees a temporary tracking number.
Connect call data to analytics and ad platforms so a call counts as a conversion.
Record calls, where legal, to review lead and sales quality by channel.

test.method: Not an A/B test; a measurement setup change.
test.measure: Calls attributed by channel and keyword

title: Add live chat with clearly stated staffed hours, not an always-on widget
hypothesis: If a live chat widget states its actual staffed hours and takes messages outside them, instead of looking permanently available with nobody behind it, then shoppers do not lose trust from an unanswered chat, because a widget that looks live but never answers reads as a broken promise.

signal.check: A live chat widget shows no stated hours and goes unanswered outside business hours.

risk.note: A settings and copy change on an existing or new widget.

prerequisites: Someone able to staff chat during defined hours
steps: Decide the real hours someone will answer chat.
Set the widget to show live status only during those hours and a message-taking mode outside them.
State the hours next to the widget.
Route unstaffed messages to email or a ticket queue with a response-time promise.

test.method: Not a test; a configuration and trust repair.

title: Check review dates for suspicious clustering before trusting review proof
hypothesis: If review dates are checked for an unnatural cluster on the same day or week, then the store catches a pattern that makes shoppers doubt the reviews, because reviews bunched around identical dates read as bought or imported rather than earned over time.

signal.check: Reviews on the PDP show many reviews dated on the same day or a narrow window, with no explanation.

risk.note: A review-request timing change.

prerequisites: Access to the review app's date data
steps: Pull the date distribution of current reviews.
Flag any unnatural cluster on one day or a narrow window.
If the cluster came from a bulk import, add context or hide the raw import date.
Space out future review requests over the normal order timeline instead of batch-sending them.

test.method: Not a test; a review-authenticity repair.

title: Add demonstration proof showing the product succeeding under the exact worry
hypothesis: If the PDP includes a photo or video demonstrating the product succeeding under the exact condition buyers worry about, then the top objection gets answered by evidence instead of a claim, because a demonstration shows the result under real stress instead of describing it in words.

signal.check: The top purchase objection from survey or review data has no matching demonstration photo or video on the PDP.

risk.note: An added media asset, easy to remove.

prerequisites: Top objection identified from post-purchase or exit survey data
Ability to produce or source a demonstration photo or video
steps: Identify the top objection from survey, review or support data.
Plan a photo or video that shows the product succeeding under that exact condition.
Produce or source the demonstration asset.
Place it in the PDP gallery near the top, not buried below other images.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test if PDP traffic is high enough.

title: Set signup and quiz forms to a middle field count with dropdowns, not free text
hypothesis: If signup, quiz and contact forms sit at a middle field count and use multiple choice or dropdown instead of free-text fields, then completion rises without the form looking like a bare data grab, because both too few fields and too many free-text fields have been linked to lower completion.
does_not_apply_when: Checkout forms, which are covered by checkout-specific field rules

signal.check: A signup, quiz or contact form has only 1 to 2 fields, has more than about 10, or uses free-text boxes where a choice would do.

risk.note: A form-field change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Access to edit the form
steps: Count the current fields and note which are free text.
Remove any field the store will not act on.
Convert free-text fields to multiple choice or dropdown where possible.
Aim for a middle field count, neither 1 to 2 nor 8 to 10 or more.
Make optional any field that is not essential to serve the shopper.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test the field count and type if traffic allows.

title: Choose PDP, advertorial, listicle or quiz format by traffic awareness level
hypothesis: If the landing format, a direct PDP, an advertorial, a listicle or a quiz, is chosen by how aware the traffic is, and unaware cold traffic gets a structured advertorial (hook, problem, mechanism, objections, proof, risk reversal, CTA), then the page argument matches what that visitor still needs, because a shopper with no context needs a different argument than one who already knows the product.
does_not_apply_when: Warm or returning traffic that already knows the product

signal.check: Cold, unaware traffic lands on a plain PDP with no story-led argument, while the ad itself carries most of the persuasion.

risk.note: A new landing page variant, tested against the existing path.

prerequisites: Knowledge of the ad angle's awareness level
Copywriting resource to build the advertorial
steps: Classify each ad concept by the audience's awareness: unaware, problem-aware, or product-aware.

For unaware or highly cold traffic, build a structured advertorial: hook in the audience's language, agitate the problem, explain the mechanism, answer about 3 common objections, show proof, offer a risk reversal, then one clear CTA.
For product-aware traffic, keep a message-matched PDP or short landing page.
Route each ad concept to the page format that matches its awareness level.

test.method: A/B test the advertorial format against the current landing path for the same ad concept, sized for the traffic.

title: Build one-of-one positioning from benefit combinations or audience white space
hypothesis: If review mining finds no unique angle, the store instead combines two real benefits into one claim or repositions the product for an underserved audience, then the product gets a differentiated position, because most products are not actually unique and free shipping, service and delivery speed are given, not differentiators.
does_not_apply_when: A genuinely unique mechanism already exists and is already the headline claim

signal.check: PDP copy strings together given benefits such as free shipping, great service and fast delivery, with no differentiated angle, and review mining found no strong unique theme.

risk.note: A positioning and copy change, easy to revert.

prerequisites: Review mining already attempted
List of the product's real benefits
steps: List every real benefit and check whether any two combine into a claim competitors cannot honestly make.
If not, look for an underserved audience the same product could serve, as a repositioning, not a new product.
Draft the new one-of-one claim from real customer words where possible.
Put the claim high on the page and move table-stakes benefits into small, low-page dot points.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test the new positioning against the current copy.
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks or at planned sample

title: Rewrite PDP feature bullets as outcome-first copy with a so-what test
hypothesis: If every feature bullet on the PDP passes a so-what test and is rewritten to lead with the outcome and follow with the feature as proof, then shoppers understand what the product does for them, because a feature list with no stated outcome makes the shopper do the translation themselves.

signal.check: PDP copy lists features such as materials, specs or ingredients with no stated outcome or benefit attached.

risk.note: A copy edit, easy to revert.

prerequisites: List of current feature bullets
steps: List every feature bullet currently on the page.
Ask so what for each one until it reaches a real outcome the shopper cares about.
Rewrite each line outcome first, feature second as the proof.
Move remaining table-stakes claims into small dot points lower on the page.

test.method: Ship as a repair, or A/B test if the page has enough traffic.

title: Choose a backlog-scoring framework by testing programme maturity
hypothesis: If the backlog-scoring framework is chosen for the programme's stage, ICE for a small team building the habit, PIE to force a look at page traffic, PXL for a mature evidence-driven programme, RICE when audience reach varies a lot, instead of using one framework by default, then the score better fits what the team actually needs to decide, because each framework trades speed for rigour differently.

signal.check: The backlog uses one scoring framework by habit, chosen with no regard for team maturity or how much reach and evidence varies across ideas.

risk.note: A process change to how ideas get scored.

prerequisites: An existing or planned idea backlog
steps: Assess programme maturity: a small team just building the testing habit, or a mature evidence-driven programme.
For a small team, use ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease) to move fast, knowing owners can inflate their own scores.
For a page-traffic-first view, use PIE (Potential, Importance, Ease), which forces a look at page traffic and value.
For a mature programme, use PXL-style evidence-gated criteria tied to heatmaps, surveys and analytics.
For ideas with very different audience reach, use RICE (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort).

test.method: Not a test; a prioritisation process change.
test.measure: Whether the scoring framework matches the programme's stated maturity

title: Turn on CUPED only with returning, identified users, not anonymous cold traffic
hypothesis: If CUPED is turned on only where the platform supports it and the store has returning, identified users to supply a pre-experiment covariate, then the store gets a real, if modest, sample-size saving instead of an assumed one, because CUPED needs a stable identity across sessions and mostly new, anonymous DTC checkout traffic gives it a missing or weak covariate.
does_not_apply_when: Mostly new, anonymous, single-session traffic with no logged-in or stable device identity

signal.check: CUPED is enabled or planned with no check for whether the tested traffic is mostly returning and identified.

expected_effect.size: vendors claim 30 to 50 percent lower sample needs on strongly correlated metrics; one large platform found only about 16 percent variance reduction on volatile revenue

risk.note: A test-engine setting, not a site change.

prerequisites: A testing platform that offers CUPED
A meaningful share of returning, identified traffic on the tested page
steps: Check whether the testing platform offers CUPED.
Check the share of returning, identified users on the page being tested.
If the share is low or traffic is mostly new and anonymous, do not expect a meaningful sample-size saving from CUPED.
If returning identified users are common, turn it on and recompute the expected sample size.

test.method: Not a test on its own; a setting decision made before sizing a test.
test.measure: Actual variance reduction observed versus the vendor's claimed range
test.read_point: After enough tests have run with CUPED on

title: Winsorize outlier orders or use a proportion metric to steady a revenue test
hypothesis: If a test's revenue metric is winsorized to cap outlier orders, or replaced with a proportion metric, then the read is steadier and needs less traffic to power, because raw average revenue per visitor is highly skewed, with most visitors spending nothing and a few large orders swinging the mean.

signal.check: A test's primary or guardrail metric is raw mean revenue per visitor with no cap on outlier orders and no pre-registered method.

expected_effect.size: unknown reduction; the method must be pre-registered, not chosen after seeing results

risk.note: A metric-definition choice, not a site change.

prerequisites: Order-level revenue data for the tested traffic
Ability to define the metric before launch
steps: Look at the order-value distribution on the tested page to see how skewed it is.
Pick either a winsorization cap on outlier order values, or a proportion metric such as purchased or not, before the test launches.
Pre-register the choice in the test brief so it is not changed after seeing results.
Apply the same method consistently across the test's catalogue.

test.method: Not a test on its own; a metric-definition step inside test sizing.
test.measure: Sample size needed with the chosen metric versus raw mean revenue

title: Layer real-time intent signals into reassurance, not only past-browsing personalisation
hypothesis: If a hesitating shopper, shown by a repeated PDP visit, cart abandonment or exit intent, sees reassurance tied to a real-time signal such as fit, shipping time, returns or compatibility, then more of them convert, because this responds to what is stopping them right now, not only to what they browsed in the past.
does_not_apply_when: Stores with too little traffic to build or justify a real-time trigger

signal.check: Personalisation on the store uses only past browsing or purchase history, with nothing triggered by the shopper's real-time hesitation signal.

risk.note: An added on-page or on-exit message, easy to remove.

prerequisites: Ability to detect a real-time hesitation signal such as repeat PDP visit, exit intent or time on page
Known top objections by category: fit, shipping, returns, compatibility
steps: Identify the top real-time hesitation signals available on the store: repeat PDP visit, exit intent, long dwell with no add to cart.
Match each signal to the objection it most likely represents: fit, shipping time, returns, compatibility.
Trigger a targeted reassurance message for that objection when the signal fires.
Keep the base page's trust signals and design solid for everyone first; treat this as a layer on top.

test.method: A/B test the triggered reassurance against no trigger, on the segment where the signal fires.
test.measure: cvr_cart_to_checkout or cvr_pdp_to_cart on the triggered segment
test.read_point: At planned sample for that segment

title: Segment AI-referred sessions in analytics before changing pages for them
hypothesis: If AI-referred sessions are segmented in analytics and compared with other channels on conversion, AOV and refund rate, then page or bidding changes for this traffic are based on its real behaviour, because AI-referred visitors reportedly convert and spend differently and start on different pages than organic search traffic.
does_not_apply_when: Stores with too little AI-referral traffic to segment meaningfully

signal.check: AI-referred traffic is not segmented in analytics, so its conversion, AOV and refund rate cannot be compared with other channels.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a measurement step, not a page change on its own

risk.note: A reporting change, not a site change.

prerequisites: Analytics able to identify AI-referral sources through referrer or UTM data
steps: Identify AI referral sources in analytics through referrer patterns or UTM tagging.
Build a segment or report comparing AI-referred sessions with other channels on landing page, conversion, AOV and refund rate.
Compare which pages AI-referred sessions land on most, often product pages, against organic search.
Use this data, not assumption, to decide whether product pages need AI-referral-specific facts.

test.method: Not a test; a segmentation and reporting step.
test.measure: Conversion, AOV and refund rate by channel, AI-referred versus others
test.read_point: Once enough AI-referred sessions accumulate to compare
